review_text:
When I first started using this cube, it felt a lot like the Rubik's brand currently available. It turns reasonably well, but that's about it. No corner cutting, etc. It's a great gift for someone that may never use it. 

 For the money, the MF3 is a LOT better cube and even challenges some cubes 3 times the price. The YJ GuanLong is also pretty good. When on sale, they are an unbelievable bargain for the quality of cube you get. 

 Overall, I wouldn't recommend this cube. Of the sub-$5 cubes, the MF3 is my favorite by far.

Overlubed with Traxxas 50k and loosen the tensions by half a turn (from stock tensions). 

 Looks: Everything is just a square. What I mean by that, well, the pieces do not have large florian holes, and the stickers aren't as rounded. Standard Moyu shades.  

 Speed: Very fast. I mean, fast enough so that it glides pretty much, but personally, I find it too fast and get some minor lockups and catches. Traxxas 50k didn't work, but it did create a very smooth feeling with the slightest gummy feeling.  

 Feel: Very smooth, very pleasant. Virtually no tactile feedback after traxxas, but w/o it, it was very bumpy at the center of the cube. Quite stable and doesn't deform from its cubic shape.  

 Corner cutting: Not great, but tolerable, just under 45 with a considerable amount of force, and 1/2 a cubie reverse with some force, not as much force as regular cc though.  

 Locks/catches: Occasionally due to competent cc. 

 Overall: A great performing budget cube. With traxxas 50k or some other high-viscous lube, it is even better.

My recommendation is to tension it good, because its tight out of the box and lube the whole puzzle with maru. Another thing to note is that its basically a non-florain modded sail. review_title: Challenging puzzle with unique shape, but mediocre stickers
review_text:
When I bought this, I thought it was a 4-color version of Tutt-Minx puzzle.  That one has pentagon and hexagon faces too (classic American soccer-ball / international foot-ball shape).  But this one I soon learned is very different.   The other puzzle has every pentagon (5 sided polygon) completely surrounded by hexagons (6 sided polygon) -- but this puzzle is the 'opposite', every hexagon is completely surrounded by pentagons!  Very unique shape!  

 This puzzle has 4 hexagon faces (each a different color) and 12 pentagon faces for a total of 16 faces (hence the name, hexadecagon).  It seems like it should be easier than Tutt-Minx which has 32 faces (12 pentagons and 20 hexagons), but I found it just as challenging -- for reasons some people may not like... 

 The most obvious thing when you get it is there are only 4 colors but 16 faces.  If there were 4 kinds of polygons that might be okay, but since only two types, there are a lot of duplicates, or at least 'almost duplicates'. 

 Some people may like the challenge, but I personally don't like when the same colors are used multiple times on the same puzzle (unless assigned to different shapes, but here duplicates do apply to the same shapes).  The problem with most such puzzles is you have to pay close attention to the order of the colors on a piece -- red / green / blue has a very different place than similar red / blue / green.  Such puzzles make me spend FAR more time than I would prefer checking colors before executing a move.  It makes things more challenging -- but in a way I find frustrating and not fun to play. 

 However, the triangular edge pieces are quite independent so the duplicates make the puzzle easier.  The trapezoid edge pieces have only 1 orientation, and they are not hard to place.  When accounting for orientation of them, you still have a pair of duplicates for each which again makes things easier.  The final issue is the corner pieces.  All corner pieces are completely interchangeable.  Again things could be very annoying with color-ordering described before, but a neat fact = trick that I soon discovered is there are 4 corner 'types' differing by missing color. 

 Confused?  Let me explain: each corner has 3 different colors, but since there are only 4 colors, it means each corner is missing 1 color.  As such, you can classify each corner by the missing color.  There are 28 corners, 7 for each class.  Most = 6 of a color class have the same color-order, for example red/green/blue while a rare 1 of a color class is different ; in this example red/blue/green.  What I did was place all 4 (only four!) 'rare' corners to their proper place, so I never had to think about color-order for the remaining corners while solving the rest of the puzzle!!  (You do still need to orient each corner piece) 

 Besides limited colors described above, the next most obvious issue is bandaging.  Many (most?) twisty puzzles don't have bandaging issues so this can surprise the unexpecting player!  If you don't know, this means that some moves which seem possible are not possible -- trying such moves will cause the puzzle to lock-up or pop pieces.  The puzzle I received didn't have any instructions on which moves are legal and which are not.  Probably because trying to describe them would be difficult ?! 

 Again this puzzle is similar to Tutt-Minx which only allows hexagon faces to be turned twice (instead of one turn) = 6 (hexagon) / 2 = 3 legal orientations of each hexagon.  With this puzzle, hexagons can be turned freely, but the pentagons are bandaged!  But things are more complex: any of the 5 orientations of pentagon are 'legal', however only 1 position allows all 5 adjacent faces to turn freely.  In other orientations, zero (0), one (1), or three (3) adjacent faces may turn freely.  This is the most tricky part to learn.  My rule: when turning a pentagon, be sure trapezoid edge-pieces align with a hexagon (if you want to turn an adjacent hexagon) and/or the triangular edge-pieces align with a pentagon (if you want to turn an adjacent pentagon). 

 The stickers seem durable, but a few were not well-placed and were rubbing / curling out-of-the box and a few more began to curl while playing. 

 The puzzle turns remarkably smoothly considering complexity, even allows some corner-cutting.  I never had any pieces pop, and it rarely jammed except when I ignored the bandaging rules (in which case it almost always jams). 

 The size is about perfect; a bit larger than the MegaMinx that I own, but smaller than my Master KiloMinx (and Void Tutt-Minx). 

 In summary, if you can tolerate bandaged puzzles with duplicate colors, then you should find this one a decent challenge.  If you're an experienced solver, it might not be much of a challenge once you learn the bandage rules.  Also the stickers should be better for the price.  In any case, it turns well enough, is well-sized, and has a very unique shape.  I enjoyed it and give it four stars.

review_title: A fun solve but turns poorly
review_text:
I was a little disappointed in the original Tangram Cube because there's just not that much to the solve. It consisted of only 3 steps and 2 of them were really easy. I'm still a fan of the overall design though so thankfully the 'extreme' version of the Tangram Cube introduces many new elements to the solve while still feeling like a Tangram Cube. It still has the same turns, the same 3 edge turns and same 2 corner turning layers, but new cuts allow the edges to now turn while the corners are offset. Not only does this create new pieces that are not present on the original cube but it also means the cube can now shapeshift as pieces can be jumbled into spots they don't belong. It provides depth to the solve that the original cube lacked.  

 The cube can be solved with a single simple alg, just like the original, but the difficulty lies in understanding the correct order of what pieces to solve next. Which is not easy when everything is all jumbled up and small triangle pieces look similar to other small yet different triangle pieces. It's a fun solve working through the logic of it and even knowing the solution it's fun just to do it. There's no orientation to worry about, just get the pieces where they need to go. 

 I have to deduct a point for how often it locks up though. There's lots of pieces of different types sliding across one another and getting stuck while turning is very common. It also can be annoying handling a cube with lots of sharp little pieces sticking out. There's a lot of little triangles on this cube and because it can shapeshift that means there's a lot of sharp little triangle points sticking out everywhere. It's not going to cut your hands up but it can be annoying at times to handle when you can't even grip it without getting poked.  

 Overall a huge improvement over the normal Tangram Cube regarding the solve but a step back regarding how it handles.

It’s an excellent puzzle, with a fun solution.

The speed is fine, and the corner cutting when testing is fine. However during solves there are some move combinations that can lead to lockups, particularly (from what I managed to gather) on slice moves. This does not happen on most of the other DaYan cubes.  

 The v1 does is also rather rigid and resistant with respect to corner cutting, but because the cube has more of a gliding feel, compared to the crispier feel of the v2, it almost becomes easier to manage. Maybe this is just a placebo effect, though. 

 On the other hand the cube does have a nice weight to it, and the turning is reasonably quick but can be set up to be controllable. Tensions came abnormally loose out of the box, even on the tightest distance setting (which by the way, is redundant due to the presence of the screw). review_title: The best cube for casual solves👑
review_text:
For casual cubers -> It's an amazing cube! It's literally made for casual cubers. Its compact so you can cube while traveling and since it pops a lot less than other 7x7s it's really nice to carry around knowing that you won't lose any pieces. And the outer texture feels a bit more like uv coating than glossy plastic but not full uv.(it's like between uv and glossy plastic) but it has some oily feeling and it can be a bit slippery but you can't really feel it when your outdoors. I had exactly two cap pops and one piece pop so far which one of the caps was actually my fault because my nail accidentally got caught between the pieces😅 But I have done like almost 50 solves and only three pops is really good for a 7x7 for this small of a size. Definitely recommend for casual cubers👍
 For speedcubers -> The reason I bought this cube was because since I only had a 3x3 and was getting a bit boring I wanted to try speedcubing big cubes. And since I go outside a lot because of studying I wanted a compact cube as well. And for some reason I thought a 7x7 was going to be the right choice to start with(which was a mistake). And when I tried the cube the turning was actually pretty good but just way too small to do some seriously fast turning like a 3x3. And realized in order to be fast with a 7x7 I needed a 65 to 67mm cube which was obviously too big to carry around. So now I only do casual solves with the 7x7 and bought a 5x5 instead to get into big cube speedcubing.
 Conclusion -> Great for casual cubing but not for speedcubing. For those who are getting into speedcubing big cubes I recommend starting with a 4x4 or 5x5 depending you want more parity or not. And don't be cocky like me and regret all decisions😅 And since these days companies like qiyi have really good budget 4x4s and 5x5s that actually perform well you can buy those ones first instead of spending over 30$ on 7x7s. I am personally a speedcuber and don't really like casual cubing but I'm not going to rate this cube low just because I'm not a casual cuber. Since this cube is probably the best choice for casual cubers.
 And one important note for speedcubers who want to try casual cubing. Don't waste money just to try casual cubing! Most speedcubers will not enjoy casual cubing as much as speedcubing. So unless you know how much you enjoy casual cubing don't try on expensive cubes👍

review_title: I'm actually impressed for the price
review_text:
Hopefully TheCubicle makes a video about this soon to explain this cube better than I can.  

 I have used TheValk 5M, DaYan Nezha 5M (Strong Magnets), and the YJ MGC 5. It might be personal preference, but I really am not sure if this cube can top them, as it feels a bit more budget. However, the UV coating on this cube makes this cube SHINE and looks amazing!  

 For anyone else curious, this cube is indeed smaller than the 3 I listed, AND it has a PRINTED logo, which I prefer much more, unlike the DaYan Nezha, but no hate towards people who do prefer sticker logos for blind/pleasure. It was just something I thought people would be curious about. 

 The outer layer magnets are a bit light, while the inner layers are moderate in terms of strength. The forward corner cutting is superb, but like the Nezha, it hardly has any reverse, if at all.  

 Additional information to those who are curious. The logo is indeed on the center piece, and the center cubies are small than the corner and the edges. I remember on DianSheng's Solar S5M, the pieces were the same sizes with the logo not on the center, so that is also an improvement. The packaging is minimal like a budget cube, and mine came a little lubed, with some lube on the outside so prepare to wipe. 

 Not a bad cube for the price, but I do not think it will be main worthy for world class solvers. 4/5 for the lack of reverse corner cutting.
Very nice mid tier cube, would prefer stronger magnets and the spring noise is abit annoying. Still working on setting it up but I am enjoying it.

review_title: Decent 5x5, But Probably Not Main-Worthy for Most People
review_text: I bought this on a whim to see how it stacked up against the Moyu Single-Track AoChuang V6. I wanted a slightly bigger puzzle between the YJ MGC (62mm), which I still enjoy, and the AoChuang (60mm), which I find a bit small for my hands. While the initial turning was decent, and the size is perfect (61.5mm), I just find the magnetic strength lacking in the inner layers. They move out of alignment much too easily, almost like a non-magnetic 5x5. I lock up during edge pairing, and while trying to do M and S moves on 3x3 stage. Adding stronger magnets would probably make this a decent contender, although I think the AoChuang's outer layers still win for speed. product_name: GAN V100 Leap 3x3 (2026 Year of the Horse Edition)
review_text:
The reason I bought it
 -This is the most amazing cube ever! I have always been a huge gan fan but the cubes were always too expensive for me to buy any good ones. But the v100 changed everything. Its performance is good as a flagship cube and it's literally half the price. It having core magnets and being 55mm was just a perfect cube that I have been wanting for years. But if you add the shipping price it was still a bit too expensive. But when they released this CNY edition I thought God literally heard what I was saying. My favorite color is orange and it was a orange internal gan v100! So I bought it immediately👍
 The review
 -Out of the box its tension is on 8 and center travel is on 3. I personally thought it was almost perfect and I think most people would just use it without needing to adjust it because it is so perfect out of the box. But since I wanted to try everything I tried to set it as loose as possible and as tight as possible. And the most loose felt like it was going to crumble as a touch it but the tightest setting wasn't actually that bad. So for people who have light turning styles would have a lot more space to adjust their prefered set up. And because it is 55mm it was perfect for my hands since I have a bit smaller hand then others. I also liked the matte finish a lot since I have very sweaty hands. For those people who don't have a clue on what matte feels like it is more like a rubbery feeling than a sandy feel. And it's great👍 The core magnets are really nice too it doesn't punish you for not doing accurate turns. And since it's spring it is much more controllable and I prefer the spring for the v100 because it's already extremely fast and I don't think it needs to be even more fast with maglev. And my favorite part was obviously the colors. For people who like orange it's a must have. It's a very bright orange and the purple magnets don't really stand out too much so if you don't like purple it still doesn't matter because it doesn't pop out as much as the orange internals. And corner cutting is also not bad but not extremely good at first. But after some breaking in the corner cutting got a lot better. If you loosen the center travel to 3 and above the corner cutting is great. But not as good ones 1 and 2.
 Conclusion
 -Overall I will give this cube a 10000000000/10 it's AMAZING. What ever your thinking if you consider buying it even a little you should definitely buy it. It won't disappoint you at all and it will probably be better than you expected. And since gan said on there social media page that it's limited in quantity you should grab it fast😃

review_text:
I'll preface this mentioning that I did have an issue with the first cube I purchased. There appeared to be a defect in the tensioning system and it wouldn't keep my settings. However, TheCubice is awesome and they sent me a replacement and I've had no issues with the new one. 

 As a fan of Matte and Springs this cube really fits me. It's fast, but controllable. Unlike the standard Gan V100, it requires a less complex lube setup to get it into a usable state for me. I've been able to dial this one in and it feels really good to solve on with just some angstrom gravitas on the tracks. 

 The matte also feels unique, it's somehow feels "softer" than other matte cubes. I don't know if that will eventually go away, but I really like the way the cube feels. 

 The only negative I would put for this cube is that it is a little flexy. Especially noticeable to me on lower tensions/compression. So I've ended up on Tension 11 and Compression 2 as I feel like this removes a bit of that flexy-ness and keeps it in cube-shape while turning fast. I assumed the tighter compression setting would mean more locking up, but I've found the opposite as it keeps the cube from flexing therefore I find it more accurate while turning. 

 I think for $30 this is a pretty great cube if you like GAN. As this cube does have that "GAN" feeling to it that most of their cubes have.

review_title: MOD THEM ALL! The V100 Perfected?
review_text:
Mods have been my favorite thing to explore lately. The Ferrocore is obviously the most glorified mod of all time (congrats guys, it's great), but it's also opened my eyes. Now that I've discovered the Picube, Zcube, and Saocube SE versions of my favorties, I'm more inclined to buy those than the originals (The Saocube Moretry is stellar btw.) 

  Here's what gets me: these weren't broken cubes. I already liked the V100, the WeiLong V10, the V11 These had little issues, the kind you accept as the cost of a flagship, or in the V100's case a flag trawler: a sturdy, non-limelight cube, out here corner cutting every day. 

 And whoever these mod wizards are, they eliminated them anyway. They took cubes I'd rate highly and elevated them. Highly recommend this one. 

 Which raises the question nobody seems to be asking: why is a third party doing the final 10% of R&D on a flagship? These companies release cubes tuned in a vacuum in their home market, while something like the V100 is popular globally, in different climates, with different setup preferences and different turning styles. The mod houses are proof there's demand for that last layer of refinement. Manufacturers should be collaborating with them, or at least learning from them. 

 Would love to see some chats with these mod houses on YouTube, Phil. Graci.

product_name: MoYu WeiLong V11 3x3 (8-Magnet Ball-Core + MagLev + Edge-Repulsion + UV PiCube SE)
review_text:
The PiCube WeiLong V11 SE is a refined take on an already excellent cube. 

 Coming from a standard WeiLong V11, the biggest difference is the stronger auto-alignment. The edge repulsion system gives the cube a noticeable snap into place, making it feel more stable and confident during solves. It’s also faster than my stock V11 while remaining very controllable. 

 What impressed me most was the out-of-the-box experience. I made no adjustments and added no lubricant—the factory setup was excellent from the start. 

 The baby-blue internals and clear core look fantastic and give the cube a premium appearance without changing the familiar V11 feel. The only downside is that some solvers may find the magnets a bit strong, especially for very fast U2 turns or slice-heavy solving. 

 I don’t see the PiCube V11 SE as a replacement for the stock V11, but rather a refined variation of it. If you’re already a V11 fan and want stronger alignment, greater stability, and a unique look, this is an easy recommendation. I’d honestly buy another one just to have a spare.

review_text: I heard this cube was good, so I bought the 20 magnet ball core with maglev. I was worried it would feel like the XT3, which I found to be uncontrollable and too flexible. It wasn't anywhere near as bad, but it was notable. It was very fast, and very flexible. I put angstrom in this cube, a little more than usual because of the cubes speed (and I find angstrom works better in cubes with primary internals than with internals that share the colors of the pieces.) I broke it in, before deciding to put it in again. I then proceeded to put some FZ calm in, before adding a ton of Silk to make it controllable, before adding FZ rush to slightly speed it up after the slowing down the silk did. After breaking in, it was still a little too fast, so I put in a bunch of Weight 5. After this, and more break in. It fits my turning style perfectly. I still need to get used to the feel of it, especially because I was using the V10 before it.  It is so soft and satisfying to turn, and I believe that is because of the Silk. It's effortless, but not fast and uncontrollable. The color shades are nice, the adjustment system is amazing, and it is a lot of fun to solve on. My LLs on it are still used to the heavier turning of the V10, but my F2L is absolutely insane. I can just do F2L effortlessly. I love it. It is an amazing cube.

review_title: Fixes My Gripes with the V11
review_text:
I really liked the V11 (20MBC) on release as it felt a lot like the GTS1. However, I had several performance issues after using it for a while. Most notably the puzzle deforming/losing its shape during algs (even after swapping the MagLev for springs), which would cause me to horribly fumble alg execution. The other big issue was the lack of range on tensions, where anything less than 8 for spring compression would make the previous issue worse.
 The Ferrocore V2's stronger magnets and spring tension system seems to help with those two issues. While I'm still experimenting with different settings and getting used to the cube, I'm doing fine on 3/6. I do notice that the FV2 does not feel as much like a GTS1 than the stock V11, but it's GTS1-esque enough for me, especially since all I needed to do for setup was dump in Traxxas 50k.
 Yes, it is a good cube and my new main, although a bit of it is due to the absurd amount of money I had to pay to get this given the state of software development, so I no longer can use my cubes as an excuse for why I perform bad.

review_title: Main-worthy after making one change to it
review_text:
For the record, I'm a solver who averages around 13-15 seconds who mains a Ferrocore V2 as of this review.
 In terms of feel I would say the plastic of the Aolong V5 has a harder feel that feels almost identical to a Weilong V10.
 Out of the box with the maglev it came with this version of the Aolong V5 is very fast to the point where I have difficulty controlling it. Even after dumping an ungodly amount of Weight 5 and Compound X into it it was still uncontrollable. 

 Eventually I decided to replace the maglev with springs, and what I got was a cube that I can get similar times on as my Ferrocore V2. In other words, replacing the Maglev with springs makes the cube a lot more manageable for someone who likes controllable cubes such as myself.
 I can very easily see myself using this cube in my next competition, and I would strongly recommend this version of the Aolong V5 if you happen to have spare Moyu 3x3 springs to replace the maglev. 

 With all this being said, I'm only going to give this cube 4 stars. Why? Firstly, the stock version with maglev is simply way too fast. Secondly, it requires a hardware change for it to have top-notch performance at least for my turning style, and not everyone happens to have spare Moyu 3x3 springs like I did. Lastly, in terms of feel I think most people (like myself) would prefer a Ferrocore V2's feel over the Aolong V5's feel any day. However, if Moyu in the future happens to release a version of this cube with springs instead of maglev I could very easily see myself giving it a 5 star review.

review_title: Not gonna break any records but...
review_text:
TLDR: Wouldn't recommend for people trying to be faster than sub-20/25, since there are better options for only a few dollars more, but a good starter 3x3/gift that's magnetic and has decent performance for only $6. 

      I bought like 6 of these to give out to friends and family who might be interested in learning how to solve the cube. Out of the box, one of the first things I noticed was the exterior finish, which seems to be just the slightest bit frosted. I was pleasantly surprised that I was able to grip and turn the cube well enough to do some algs relatively well, whereas a lot of cubes in this price range come dry and slippery to the point of almost being unusable for any speedcubing whatsoever. 
      The tensions were also even and quite reasonable (Can get an edge out without too much difficulty, but don't think it'll pop). I did a few solves and got some meh results due to some random lockups here and there. I decided to do some minor setup, which basically just involved cleaning out the factory lube, and using weight 5 on the core, tracks, and pieces, and tightening each screw by a quarter turn.
       The end result was a moderate speed, blocky cube with a slight crunchy feel. I still wasn't able to get amazing times on it, but I don't really think that's the purpose of this cube. As far as I'm aware, the quality control and out of the box usability, combined with the price tag of this cube make it a straightforward option for someone wanting to spend a minimal amount of money on a magnetic cube!

review_title: I wanted to love this cube
review_text:
I'm legally blind. I actually got into cubing because my fiancée bought me this dice-numbered cube figuring I'd appreciate it as a novelty. ADHD kicked in and … I learned the ruwix beginner alg and was hooked. But the dice number cube isn't good for fast solving, so I typically use a normally colored cube. 

 This SHOULD be the ideal cube for a blind solver, and even I could benefit from the tactile color cues (never mistake yellow for white in suboptimal lighting again!) But … it's not. 

 First, the pieces do not line up evenly. Which means they catch and snag on each other. Second, some of the pieces have pronounced cheap plastic feel where the parts that make up a given edge/corner come together. It's a combination of cheap plastic and lack of attention to the polish you'd get on other cubes like the RS3M V5 Standard or even the Meilong 3M. 

 Can you fix it? Sure. Time, sandpaper, a little glue maybe to keep pieces from separating. Might as well glue some magnets in there while you're at it. Enough TLC and this would be a fine cube! But that's not something a new blind cuber is going to be able to do, which means out of the package this cube isn't ready to rock. 

 Which is too bad because the pieces are very nicely textured. (Doesn't matter the orange hearts are facing all different ways, the question is how fast can you tell them from the other shapes? Immediately, that's how fast.) And these aren't stickers on the cube, they're colored plastic bits that snap into the black pieces. That part is quite excellent. So a little polish on this thing could've gone a long way toward the ideal product for the audience. I'm sorry this is reportedly the best out there for us. 

 Bottom line: If you know a blind person and you want them to try cubing, grab a mirror block. The Gan mirror block, ideally, since it's the only one that has magnets as of this writing. The magnets help a great deal with that thing, even if I wish they were a little stronger. 

 But this product? Unless you want to take the time to provide the polish that the factory didn't, it's going to be a little underwhelming. Still kinda cool, but a little underwhelming. 

 YJ … what does it take to make this a cube a person could compete with out of the factory? I realize it'd cost more than this if you made it. Still, if you or someone else does make such a cube, I'm buying it. Because the concept you've got here is very excellent. I just want a better execution please.

 I love the way the zhilong line feels... However this 7x7 is disappointing compared to what I am used to with this line of cubes.  

 If you're looking for a small budget 7x7 thats great for speedsolving, the Warrior M is going to be your best bet. That cube just got the ASR and WR2 single. 

 The YJ pocket 7x7 is overall a fun cube to solve, its small, light, fast, and mostly enjoyable to solve. I like the way the cube feels but it has some serious stability issues, even after tightening. It has popped or had a major lockup on every solve I have done, even after tightening. It has similar stability issues to older big cubes (or older cuboids like Witeden's) where you tighten the centers and the middle layers are tight, but the outer edges are still loose and can pop out a lot easier than you would like.  

 I'm disappointed by this cube and I was really looking forward to a better 7x7 from this line of cubes. I was really hoping this 7x7 would be around the 60mm size mark instead of 55mm. It's 3mm smaller than their 5x5 in the same lineup of cubes. 

 This cube is just too small to be something I would really want to solve with.  

 As for the portability of it... It's very portable but due to the instability I would not trust this cube enough to solve it in public or in areas where pieces could get lost forever easily.  

 This puzzle is cheaper than the Diansheng mini 7x7 which is a bonus, but I still think it's overpriced for what you're getting. It's a watered down 7x7 that's too small for no reason. 

 I'd like to rate this puzzle higher but due to the stability issues, size, and price, it does not feel worth it. I was hoping this cube release wasn't going to be aimed towards "novelty" considering how well their other cubes preform in this line.

review_title: A fun little novelty, but be careful
review_text:
First of all, I wanted this cube just because I thought it would be fun to have a 7x7 that's roughly the same size as most standard 3x3s. It definitely delivered on that aspect, and the turning ended up exceeding my expectations, which had been set by horror stories about mini big cubes (is that an oxymoron?) of the past, namely the FangShi Mini 6x6. 

 However, while it can be tempting to turn quickly and be a little more reckless, it's important to be extra careful with making sure that each layer is properly aligned before starting the next turn. I instinctively tried to corner cut once and got a nasty lockup, and while attempting to remedy it, a large portion of the cube exploded all over the room. Thankfully the magnets somewhat lightened the challenge of reassembly, but let this be a warning to anyone who plans on seriously speedsolving with this thing. With the cube's much smaller size, I wouldn't have been surprised if I ended up losing a piece or two. 

 Overall, this is a surprisingly competent puzzle for being a tiny 7x7, and while it definitely works as something to occupy my hands when I'm bored, it won't be replacing my main any time soon.

Turning could be smoother, corner cutting could be easier, but it's good enough to get a sense of speed with precise turning.

review_title: Excellent modern Square-1, unfairly compared to the legendary V1
review_text:
Honestly, this Square-1 is excellent. I can totally understand why some longtime MGC SQ-1 users may not like it as much, especially if they are used to the original hardware, which became an absolute legend in the Square-1 community. But if you judge this cube for what it actually is, it’s really good. 

 The turning feels smooth and modern, the puzzle is stable, and the UV coating gives it a great premium feel in the hands. For someone who wants to get into Square-1 or start learning the event seriously, I honestly think this is one of the best choices available right now. 

 In my opinion, this cube’s biggest problem is simply being compared to one of the greatest Square-1s ever made. Because of that, some people overlook how solid this V2 actually is. Taken on its own, it’s a fantastic puzzle and absolutely deserves recognition.

review_title: A fine cube with two minor niggles
review_text:
It turned much more smoothly out of the box than the 5-layered version I bought a few months ago, which is a surprise as I always thought cubes with internal pieces always turned worse than cubes without them. It turns so smoothly it even has a bit of corner cutting, which the 5-layered version doesn't have. The solve was fun and the parity can be worked out intuitively.  

 But one issue I had was that the cube came pre-lubed with lube smeared all over the internal white pieces but since they show on the surface on each face, every time I turn the cube I inadvertently touch the white pieces and get lube on my fingers. Since this cube has hidden screws and thus can't be taken apart it makes wiping off that lube a challenge. 

 Also, it's a bit stiff, especially when you try to turn the corners, and since I can't access the screws, I can't loosen it. Hmm...

It's one of my favorite puzzles now. There's a new parity issue that can occur that doesn't exist on a 4x4 cube or master pyraminx, but it's pretty easy to prevent once you understand how it happens. Made for a lovely challenge to first time solve with no help. If you can do a Jing pyraminx and 4x4 cube, it's a fun puzzle. Only complaint is the turning quality. It's a lot tighter than it's 5 layer counterpart and I can't figure out how to access the screws on it.

review_title: Higher order version of Jing Pyraminx
review_text: The turning is alright, the outer turns are better than the inner turns, but it still doesn't turn as well as the 5-layered version. At first, I wasn't having a lot of fun when I got parity because tetrahedrons work very differently from cubes. You can get the color scheme correctly and still get center parity because of how the inner pieces work. And if you solve the centers in that state, it gives you a single corner twist parity. I sat down and tried some things, and I eventually figured out how to twist a single corner. The algorithm I came up with is long, but it's the same 4 moves done 10 times, it's tedious but easy. I had a pop when I tried to turn too quickly, it's not a speed cube, just a regular puzzle, still fun though.

 Because of that comparison, I can’t give the Vin Cube a full 5-star rating. That doesn’t mean it’s a bad cube—far from it. I’m sure a lot of people will really enjoy it. The stickerless version does not have this, thus each color has 3 pieces that are exactly the same and can be swapped about without any issues.  If you want a better challenge, go with the stickered version.

I really like this puzzle! First off, note that this is NOT the same puzzle as a master skewb. It looks identical but turns and solves differently. 4 corners turn with shallow cuts, and the other four have deeper cuts that turn like a master skewb (as well as trivial tips). This is a moderately difficult puzzle that has elements of many other corner turning puzzles such as a skewb, dino cube, rex cube, FTO, and even pyraminx and master pyraminx to some extent. After a little effort, I was able to figure out how to solve it. I can now solve in with a couple different methods. After playing around wiht it for the first 15 minutes or so, I had a major realization about this puzzle (although it still took much longer after that to solve it). I won't go into details on what this realization was or how I solved it. If you want that you can go on Youtube and find a tutorial. I'd say this is basically the same difficulty as a rex cube or FTO. It's not a puzzle for someone brand new to twisty puzzles. If you're comfortable solving other mid-level non-WCA puzzles, this should take a bit of thinking but not be insanely difficult. In order to solve this, you need to know how to solve a dino cube and a skewb, and be comfortable with basic 4-move commutators (A B A' B') and conjugates/setup moves (A B A', where B is usually multiple moves, and A sometimes is). You don't really need to come up with any of your own algorithms, or use any 8 move commutators. Turning quality is perfectly adequate for a non-speedcube. The puzzle has no issues with turning as long as you're not trying to speedsolve it.

First off, be warned this is not the same puzzle as the Lanlan master skewb. This is essentially a master F-skewb. That being said, if you are a non-wca lover or collector, this is must have. It is a stable puzzle. It has a dayan feel (lighter plastic) and the turning is good out of the box. To solve this you will need to be able to solve a skewb, dino cube, Rex cube and know commutators.

This can take a bit to wrap your head around just how it moves and what puzzles it can be reduced to -- it's not intuitive at first but once you start diving into it and figuring it out it's a very rewarding solve. 

 I'd recommend this to anyone who has experience with a bunch of other non-WCA 4-axis and 8-axis puzzles.  If, however, you just learned to solve a skewb and are looking for something "just a little harder," bookmark this one and come back to it later, get some experience with a rex cube and maybe a master pyraminx or even an FTO and then take on this one — this one is the kind of puzzle that I think you're going to enjoy more if you're able to come up with your own solution rather than falling back on a tutorial. 

 Turning quality is good.  It'll catch at times but nothing that should impede your solve.

review_title: Challenging puzzle, great quality, fair price
review_text:
I've solved many "harder" puzzles before, but not this one yet!  I think I know solution, but my algorithms are not very efficient so it solving is slow. 

 Unlike other reviews, my puzzle has never popped!  I'm not afraid to say it (as some other of my reviews do).  I don't know if DanYan improved the mechanics or prior reviewers got a "bad batch". 

 In fact, this is one of the few (only?) puzzle that I give full 5 stars.  Things I like:
 * 6 classic colors of original Rubik's cube (in the same orientation)
 * Sticker quality is nearly perfect (I can't think of any flaws, but there might be some very minor ones)
 * Size and weight nearly the same as classic Rubik's cube (good!)
 * Each face has 8 facets, one less than standard Rubik's cube, but there is no fixed center, so arguably same 
 * Very challenging, at least for me
 * Turns smooth out-of-the-box (even though it seems not lubricated)
 * Nice price (not the cheapest puzzle, but there are more expensive puzzles with worse performance/quality) 

 The bad:
 * Will sometimes lock-up, especially if you get in a hurry (I don't think lube would help, but haven't tried)
 * nothing else :) 

 I guess if you tried to aggressively turn it like a speed-cube you might pop pieces?  After spending a few days trying to solve it (without success) I decided to take it apart, to see how it works and start over from a "new" state.  It took considerable effort to get a piece to pop to begin disassembly.  WARNING: if you try this, only remove a few pieces at a time!  After removing 6 to 8 pieces (as I recall) the entire thing will disintegrate, and is a REAL challenge to re-assemble. 

 Hints/suggestions: this is shaped like a cube, but has 4 axes of rotation, like a tetrahedron... in other words a disguised (master)Pyraminx!  I strongly suggest you master the basic Sqewb first!  I can solve that, but this one is still a challenge.  I guess if you can solve this easily, it is time for the Master Sqewb?  This one actually costs more than Lan Lan Master Sqewb, but I haven't bought that yet, so it may be worth the price? 

 Anyway, I love it, and recommend as either good challenge or a nice addition to a collection.

review_title: Stiff turning, but a fun solve
review_text: It took me a long time to decide to give this puzzle a chance, as I've heard all the worst reviews about it, about how horribly it turns, how much it pops, etc. I think the puzzle came out at least 2-3 years ago (it's now May 2021), and I've just now purchased it. So, what can I say? Having done two full solves on it, along with some isolated Compy Cube and Skewb solves, along with just playing around with it, I can say that my very low expectations have been exceeded. The Skewb turns are fairly reasonable, with minor catching. Half of the Dino turns are alright as well. The other half of the Dino turns are the main problem, as they are very stiff and catchy - however - if you're careful, it's functional enough where you can do a solve without a pop. I've been careful with it and so far I haven't gotten a single pop, thankfully. The catchiness and stiffness can be a bit frustrating, but considering that this is a one-of-a-kind hybrid puzzle of a Compy Cube and a Skewb, I think it's still worth it. If you're a speed cuber and only like smooth turning puzzles, then this puzzle may not be for you. But if you don't mind some stiffness and catchiness and enjoy unique challenging solves, and know how to handle such a puzzle carefully to minimize the chances of a pop, then I'd recommend it.

review_text:
Even though i've heard a lot of people saying that this puzzle is horrible, i still wanted to buy it because i simply loved the concept. When i first receive this puzzle it has been lubed quite a bit so the all of the cuts turned relatively well (mine's a stickered version so can't say anything about the other two). The stickers at the small tips were an actual problem. Due to their small size they're easy to fall off if you're not careful enough. And even if it pops it's quite easy to put the pieces all back in unlike other higher order puzzles, but you need to make sure they're in the right place or else you'll get a few impossible "parities" while solving it. 
 If you still want to buy this puzzle then choose the stickerless version (if you still want the stickered version than you should buy some extra stickers or something like that), and try to tighten it a bit more rather than loosen it, because if not it'll just make the puzzle pop even more frequently. Oh and don't forget to lubricate it as well if you can.

review_title: Puzzle is a nightmare to move and put back together
review_text: Chances are the pieces are going to catch when you try to scramble/solve this puzzle. Several times I had to stop moving the puzzle because I was afraid it was going to pop. And guess what? That's exactly what happened. Putting that monstrosity back together used up ALL of my patience. I'll just add this puzzle to my collection of "Never Scramble These Puzzles Again."

Avoid this puzzle at all costs, unless all you want is to put it on a shelf. 

 I wasn't expecting a speed cube. I wasn't even expecting something that would move all that well. But I was expecting something I could at least scramble and solve, even if it maybe had a lot of catching in the process. What I got was something that simple can't be used. Period. Over the course of 5 minutes, I was able to rotate each of the layers in one direction 120 degrees each, and then return them. That's 12 turns, 4 of which are trivial twists of the corners, over the course of 5 minutes. Even going that slowly and carefully, I had pieces pop out multiple times. The fact is that this isn't a puzzle at all - it's just a bunch of plastic pieces that interlock into a cube. 

 Aside from the turning (or lack thereof), this doesn't even look good on a shelf. The product image on this page uses very flat lighting, which limits how visible it is, but with real life lighting, the fact that every piece is sitting at a slightly different elevation/angle makes it look awful, and there's no "straightening it" that you can do to fix it, as the central 9 squares on each face will always be raised relative to the others. 

 I have well over 200 puzzles in my collection. I've gotten some pretty bad ones in the past that I know better than to try to scramble. Still, I have never had one bad enough that I ended up returning it. Until now.

review_title: A bad design is the “Center of Attention”
review_text:
Did you know that center piece is composed of TEN different individual parts? They are:
 -Center body
 -Center stalk
 -Magnet for MagLev
 -Center to core lock nut
 -Center travel adjustment ring
 -Compression adjustment ring
 -Cap retainer
 -3 exterior color caps
  That is absolutely wild. Makes setup extremely difficult. When you have the cube taken apart down to the core and centers, the lock nut doesn’t do a very good job among keeping the center from falling off the core. To put it back on the core, you must remove the corner cap to get the lock nut in place.  

 But wait, that’s not the end of it. The center stalk is not attached to the rest of the center piece. The cap is also incredibly tight and extremely difficult to get off. Many times you can grip the stalk of the piece and use that as leverage to pull the cap off. Nope. The stalk just falls off and you have no leverage to remove a center cap.  

 In the end, the cap was so tight that the yellow colored piece ended up breaking. All down to a poor and overcomplicated design that is more difficult to take apart and reassemble than an Audi Q5.  I’m buying another one. But I’ll give it credit, it is a very good performing puzzle.

Buy this cube if you have accurate turning style and can handle fast maglev cubes. Cube is great for beginners.

review_title: Wonderful, but tricky & risky to adjust
review_text:
This cube has wonderful action, it blows away most cubes that are 2-2.5x its price. Very smooth fast turning & very little catching. It is amazing that somebody makes this nice & adjustable of a cube for this price. Personally I still prefer my Swift Block MagLev & Super MagLev better - they are faster, easier and stress-free to adjust, and same price-point. But if you want max adjustability for <$20, and don't mind tricky adjustment, you can't beat this at twice the price.  

 Adjusting is very risky and fiddly. I would only give it 4⭐️ if it cost as much as equivalent cubes, but at this price that would be ridiculous. 

 Each adjuster nuts is 3 tiny pieces, and they popped off by accident & flew all over the place several times b/c of the maglev repulsion, just from trying to adjust. It would be very easy to lose a piece, and would then be junk - I wish it came with spares, I was genuinely stressed while adjusting it. Definitely use the screwdriver to turn the dial, don't do it by hand. Even with that, it was hard to get the dial into the 1 position, for tension, it kept over-shooting. 

 I also don't like the fact that you have to remove a center piece and deal with the risk of losing an adjuster nut part, to disassemble it & get at the corner-core magnets to adjust them. But I do like that you just turn those to adjust them instead of having to swap out magnet posts like a lot of GANs.
DaYan GuHong Pro+ 3x3 54mm (MagLev)

review_text: This FTO has been long awaited by FTO enthusiasts for many many months. The diansheng was okay, but it just popped way too much, causing many sessions to be filled with and end in despair. This dayan FTO completely fixes that issue, with a puzzle that is literally impossible to pop. The feeling is a bit heavier and a bit more stable than the diansheng, and doesn't work as well with lube, but it makes up for it in terms of how well it performs. its corner cutting is a lot better than the diansheng, and the ball core makes for a more smooth turning experience. I think the size is a bit too big, perhaps 2-3 mm smaller would be perfect. but it is such a joy to solve on. I have done well over 2,500 solves at this point, and not only has it not come close to ever popping, but i have been able to break so many pbs with it, including a 11.26 WB3 single (at the time), 14.10 ao5, 15.12 ao12, and 16.74 ao100. all top 3 or 4 in the world! I have also gotten 2 more sub 12s since the pb single, and i just can solve on this all day long. i cant wait to see more top performing FTOs. if you are serious at all about FTO, please do not hesitate to get this.
I got this cube and was averaging sub-2:00 within 2 days of having even learned to solve it. Great puzzle!

review_title: Definitely the Best FTO Out There
review_text:
There are already so many positives about this cube so I won't write them down. 

 Some flaws about this cube is that it is a bit big for me (QiYi size is ideal), it does not go good with lube, loose tensions come with too many lockups and some corner twists, and the cube is just slow. One factor that makes the cube slow is that the magnet layout makes the magnets attract halfway through a turn, to fix this I've came up a solution by changing the magnet layout without making the cube flimsy: to flip one of the triangle to edge magnets and flipping the corresponding edge magnets, making it repel at halfway like the MGC Repulsive.  

 Overall though, the other FTOs in the market pales in comparison to the DaYan but there could still be improvements in further FTO hardware and I hope that other companys start mass producing FTOs.

review_title: Skip this one and get the 5x5
review_text: The Diansheng 5x5 minx is simply amazing, but the 4x4 is not. The clamshell shape of the edge pieces make the turning chunky, the lack of magnets on the middle layer make the outside layer sticky, and the whole thing feels like it wants to pop. I can't recommend the 5x5 version of this cube highly enough, and if you really want a 4x4 minx, go with the ShengShou

review_title: A Must-Have Cube For Many Of Us
review_text: Yes, it's a 2x2 shape mod...but to be more accurate...it's a Pyramorphix shape mod (photo #1 shows the Flymouse next to a pillowed Pyramorphix turned 90 degrees).  If you enjoy 2x2 shape mods then you'll want to get this unique puzzle...which is basically a 2-color Pyramorphix with no easy corner pieces. Hint: try solving it as you see it in photo #2...with the 4 big pieces on the bottom and the 4 small pieces on top. This upright position will be much easier to achieve than trying to reach the truly solved state where the cube is lying flat. I think of the 4 big pieces as the "legs" and once I solve the first layer I turn the cube over and stand it on its legs in order to solve the top. One twist from the upright position and the cube is fully solved. For fun, try creating the odd, plant-like shape in photo #3...believe it or not it's only 4 moves from the solved state. I've purchased this puzzle in both colors, so that will tell you how much I love it.
My 9-year-old loves his Flymouse.  Initially he was worried when he scrambled it, but got it figured out and now it is one of his favorites.

While the flymouse is a shape mod of a basic 2x2x2 puzzle, it gives a much more visually dynamic experience that invites you to solve it differently.  The turning will sometimes catch a little, but it otherwise feels and turns well.  It's a lot of fun for such a simple puzzle. 

 Also, the flower shape can function as an orange juicer (note: not actually tested or recommended).

review_title: Pretty easy, but a great spinner and a cute little puzzle
review_text:
As a spinner, it's great. I set it to spinning on the table, went off to have a conversation with my wife, got back, and it was still going. Neat! And fairly quiet. 

 As a puzzle, it's really simple. Like the other fidget spinner puzzles, it's quite a bit more sturdy than a regular floppy puzzle, probably owing to having a strong metal core in the middle there. That's actually why I bought it, I like the floppies but don't like picking up little pieces of plastic off my floor. 

 Anyway, as a puzzle, it's simple but pleasant. The corners basically have no orientation, so a greedy algorithm can solve them all, then you can sort of clean up the edges at the end (there is likely a more optimal solution if you find yourself in a contest situation, which I find unlikely). But it's a nice little puzzle, and for the price, I enjoyed it.

review_text:

On the other hand, the magnets in the Diansheng feel stronger, which also makes it feel pretty bumpy. 

 I've had one pop (one of the hidden centers) while scrambling aggressively, but none so far during solves. I've seen someone else have this same pop during a solve in a review video, so I don't know if it's going to be a big issue. Adjusting the tension might help. I haven't used the old Diansheng, so I can't make comparisons to that. 

 Both the Dayan and the Diansheng are good, but not 5-star. They're both kinda bumpy and clackety, and the corner cutting is not great. If you catch, they flex and bunch up in an annoying way. There isn't any FTO hardware that has the smoothness and features seen in comparable WCA puzzles. With companies like GAN dipping their toes into stuff like Mirror Cubes, hopefully we'll get some more FTO options in the near future. 

 In the mean time, this is the best FTO on the market for me. If you have large hands, or prefer a slower, smoother feel, the Dayan might be better for you.

review_title: Innovative, but with Room for Improvement
review_text:
I understand the hype for the first ever speed FTO- I love the stickerless tiles; the colors and the scheme get no complaints from me; and magnets are great. This was sorely needed, I'm glad it exists, and I'm glad I have it.
 However, the mechanism leaves much to be desired. Only the edges properly engage with the core, and I still don't understand what black magic holds the triangles and corners in place on top of them. It pops a lot out of the box, and the screws are really buried in the mechanism, so I'm not super inclined to mess with it- I fear after tightening it, reassembly may be even more difficult, and if I tighten it unevenly, it would take that much more time to correct.
 If you buy it, be ready to reassemble it a lot. I recommend to build it in blocks, and when in doubt, do edges first and triangles last. 
 This is the first; if diansheng and other manufacturers see the room for improvement and capitalize, then the future is bright for the FTO community :)

I've seen many reviews of this puzzle and waited with high anticipation for mine to arrive. I know that many other reviewers have said the tension needs to be slightly adjusted out of the box, and that the puzzle has popping problems due to the design of the internals. I have not had any of those issues myself. For me, the puzzle felt great right out of the box and it has not popped even once. On the other hand, I am not a particularly fast solver or fast/aggressive turner. If I had faster turning or relied on more finger tricks for FTO, it's quite possible I would have encountered these problems. But if you're still kinda slow like me, this puzzle will probably serve you absolutely as well as you need. The only thing stopping me from giving it the full five stars is that a) the gray side color is kind of an ugly, brownish gray. I've gotten used to it, but I wish it was a more neutral gray or even black. b) the issues with the design of the puzzle's internals are real--even if they haven't affected me personally--so I know there's room for Diansheng to improve. I look forward to them doing so! 

 But all that aside: if "I'm waiting for better hardware" has been your reason for not getting into FTO up to now, you need wait no further. We have been waiting for a speedsolving FTO for *years*, and Diansheng delivered. More than that; they didn't just deliver a puzzle that is speed-solvable. They delivered a speedsolvable puzzle that is actually *good*. It may not be at the same level of awesome/fast/reliable as modern 3x3 hardware (yet!) but this is a 100% legit puzzle that brings a true speedsolving experience to FTO.

review_title: Good but too much work to set up
review_text:
This is a good puzzle with solid construction with one major caveat. As other reviewers have noted, there is flash (a little hanging chad) on the + centers (the center pieces directly adjacent to the main centers. Only after clipping and sanding this on all 60 of these center pieces does the puzzle perform as intended. While doing this I also noticed some corrosion on one of the screws.  

 I know that puzzles require setup but this is an excessive amount of extra work for a $60 puzzle.  

 After doing all this it feels great to solve.
Big fan of the quality! I have certain megaminx’s that don’t turn as well as this puzzle!

At the time of writing this review, I currently hold the world best for gigaminx with a 5:07 single. This puzzle is by far the best currently on the market for speedsolving gigaminx. It's much smaller than other gigaminxes, actually only 2 or 3 mm larger than the Yuhu megaminx, but it doesn't feel too small when solving. The magnets are great and help a lot with turning the layers you want to turn. The turning is crisp, smooth, and fairly fast with lube. I loosened the puzzle by a quarter turn from the factory tensions. The puzzle does have some issues with pops and lockups where pieces come out of place and sometimes these lockups kill a solve, but generally they're pretty manageable. The biggest issue with this puzzle in my eyes is the flash on the + centers. Each and every one had a bit of extra plastic where there shouldn't be any plastic, causing catching issues. I removed all of this flash using nail clippers and the performance improved noticeably. This was pretty easy to do and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone wanting to speedsolve this puzzle. Overall, the puzzle loses some points for occasional bad lockups and the clear design flaw of flash on the + centers, which is why I'm giving 4 stars instead of 5, but this puzzle is really amazing and turns far better than any other gigaminx currently on the market. If you're only interested in casual solving and not speedsolving, I'd just get the Yuxin as it's much cheaper and still turns well enough. For speedsolving, this is absolutely the way to go.

review_title: A step in the right direction
review_text:
This suffers from a lot of the usual issues that even-layered puzzles suffer from. OOTB, it was terrifyingly loose, and once it was tightened it is the single lockiest 'speed' puzzle that I have. The magnets are stronger in the outer layer than the inner, which is reverse from what it usually is. This undoubtedly contributes to it's locking problem. This was done because there is a very limited size of magnet that can be installed in the inner layers. The solution was not to keep small magnets in the inner layers and normal ones in the outer, but to put even smaller magnets in the outer, because having them backwards like this does not serve the puzzle's performance any good.  

 Minxes are my favorite style of puzzle, and this is probably the best master kilominx currently, but more innovation is needed for this puzzle. This is a step in the right direction, but there is much more work do be done.

review_title: Caught and fell apart on my first solve
review_text:
This is not my first rodeo, I've had delicate non-WCA puzzles before. But this was so hyped up, I had pretty high expectations. I was turning slowly; it's a little catchy, but it's alright. The solve was going well. I was excited to figure out how parity was going to work on a minx. 

 But then I got a catch I couldn't quickly resolve. It turns out the core inside isn't solid, it's made of a ton of little pieces gently arranged together, and one of those pieces got out of alignment. I can't really see where it's supposed to go, but I tried to get it back into position; when I did, a larger (internal, hard to see) piece fell inside the center and disappeared, along with the one I was trying to fix. 

 For $42 in the year 2025, I really do expect better. I was very excited to finish my collection and this is just ... sitting in pieces on my table. It's too new even for there to be youtube videos on how to put it back together, so it's just sitting there until I have two hours to figure this out, I guess. I really can't recommend it.

review_title: Amazing cube once properly set up
review_text:
I've had this thing for a while now, and I agree with the other commenter. OOTB it was a horrible experience and I was extremely disappointed at first. 

 DianSheng made it difficult for themselves by going for a design without the very prominent black "star" in the middle. I prefer this design, but it's also the reason the cube performs so poorly at first, tiny magnets in the middle pieces, and the center pieces are shaped in a way that the part that extends to the middle goes over the other pieces when turning. That makes it extremely catchy and the middle layers almost always turned with the outer layers, which became annoying fast. 

 I played around with the screws a lot and found that just tightening the screws slightly helped the most, lubed it with Mystic and put some Compound X only between the middle layers, careful not to slow it down too much and added a touch of DNM to the outer layers. 

 And after a few hundred solves I can confidently say that all of the issues I had with it at first are practically gone. For an even-layered dodecahedron this is an amazing puzzle if you give it a chance.

review_title: The original, but cheaper and more adjustable.
review_text:
The Guhong Pro+ M is essentially a V2 of the original Guhong Pro M, and it's somehow cheaper (by a dollar). It has the same feel as the original, but the magnets feel a bit stronger (Probably the Maglev version only). The turning is great, and it has that "Dayan Feel" (Papery and Soft), it cuts well, and the slices feel nice. The center caps feel much more snug, which fixes one of the problems some users had with the original Guhong Pro, where they came off easily. The upgrade is worth it, coming from someone who used the original Guhong Pro as their main (56 Standard).
 But this version features a Dual-Adjustment system and adjustable corner core magnets (Dual Adjustment was needed for sure). The Dual Adjustment system has the same qualities as the Tornado v3, being able to adjust both the Tension and the Compression with the same gear, as well as being "hand-adjustable" to an extent (they provide a screwdriver for the system for ease of use). However, the numbers are hard to read at a glance since the numbers are small, as well as the plastic being clear and dark purple. It's not as good as the TV3, but it's nice and functional. The adjustable Corner Core magnets are also a nice touch (if I'm not mistaken, it makes it the cheapest cube with corner core magnets that are adjustable). They also function well, you can feel the strength increasing the higher you go.

review_title: Compact, Fast, and a Personal Favorite
review_text: This is one of my favorite cubes from the order. I really like how compact the 54mm size is while still performing at a high level. It’s especially good for one-handed solving, and I sometimes switch to it as my main for 2 hand solving but main it for one hand solving. It’s probably the best small cube I’ve used and one of the best budget cubes overall. The only downside is that it’s not super customizable, but even with that, it performs really well.
I’m spinning the wheels off this cube. For the price this cube is very good. Turns smoothly with hardly any lockup. When I get use to a cube it becomes my favorite and this cube is now my favorite.

This cube is great. The manual teaches ALL of cfop, the packaging is so good, (especially how the box opens). And on top of that, this is better than most flagships. It's very fancy, and I love the orange core. The cube's size also fits my hands. One issue is that it's too oily, but nothing a napkin can't fix. Overall, this is probably my favorite 3*3.

It's very fast, and I can get very fast TPS because of that and the smaller size (I have smaller hands). I like that you can choose which size it is. I have seriously thought of using this as my main. Seriously, I think that this is better than the RS3V5. I love the smooth and quick plastic feel. After break-in it has noticeable auto-alignment, but it's not too much to where it's intrusive, it just gives a small "push" at the end of my turns. I average 17 seconds on 3x3, but with this cube I have been popping off 16 second averages. I would recommend this cube to any cuber of any skill level.

The Guhong Pro+ is an even better version of the original Guhong Pro. The feeling is quite similar, though I believe that the Guhong Pro+ is more smoother than the Guhong Pro.  

 The Pro+ has more features, which is great because I thought that the magnet strength on the Pro was a bit lacking, so it's great to be able to adjust that. For tension and elasticity settings, I like mine on more looser settings, and they do not disappoint. Tighter settings work fine too, if you want a more controllable cube. 

 Out of the box, the cube felt great, mainly due to the Dayan lube, but I hate how the cube is quite literally DUMPED in lube (I'm assuming). Corner cutting is almost never an issue, and when I do get lockups, it's more due to my inaccurate turning and not the cube. 

 I got the 54mm maglev version, as I did with the original Guhong Pro, and this cube just expands on the already great performance of the Guhong Pro, but with more options of customizations and at a cheaper price! 

 Overall, I would heavily recommend this cube to anyone, Beginner or Pro.

 2: it has pretty weak magnets, so it can be quite unstable
 3: You're pretty limited on where to lube the pieces. Only the tracks and top 3rd of the inner pieces contact with each other. I was pretty disappointed about that :( 

 I did some mods on this by gluing stronger magnets in the corners and stuffing every piece full of foam. It felt much more controllable and solid after that, and a combo of weight 5, dignitas, and Fz calm makes it so soft to the point where I can barely hear it while turning as fast as I can! By far the most satisfying cube I have and will probably ever feel! The lube keeps running out quick though, I think because it's all going to the spots where the pieces don't touch. :/ 

 Other than that though, I'd say this cube is very light, soft, and effortless to turn. I can execute PLL faster on this cube than on any other. It's REALLLY flexible too. I can stretch it open to the point where the cube explodes! (IDK if that's a good or bad thing...) So no need to worry about corner cutting. OOTB tensions are pretty good already.  

 In conclusion, this cube is pretty good OOTB and INCREDIBLE if you want to spend just a little time and effort by putting stronger magnets in it and, if you're hardcore like me, some foam or something similar into the pieces to make it less hollow. Great cube! Softest I've ever felt. :)

My only complaints about this cube are the magnets, which can be solved easily with a RS3M magnet kit, and the yellow looks kinda weird. But overall I'm super satisfied with this cube, even if it is like 5 years old.

review_title: Fantastic Cube but a Couple Problems
review_text: The DaYan Guhong Pro M is a great cube but I would like to note some issues. Firstly, DaYan drenches all of their cubes in lube for some reason, which is why it feels amazing out of the box but it also is all over the outside of the cube and continues to leak out for the first day or two of usage. Now secondly, there is something wrong with the corner magnets at least in my cube. One of them came loose during a fast-turning PLL and it made shaking noises. I took it out of the corner piece but now I am not sure how to put it back in properly. Since that incident, other corner piece magnets have came loose and made noise for a few seconds but then fall back into place and it is quite annoying. I am not sure if this has happened to anybody else but even if there is a fix it seems to keep happening and I am not sure what to do. You can only adjust centre distance which isn’t that big of a deal, but the cube can feel very flimsy at times with cheap airy feeling plastic. The only other downside that I feel like doesn’t really get talked about is it’s lack of decent corner cutting - it struggles with a 45 degree, and can’t quite do line to line reverse. Even with all these downsides considered, man it really is just one of the most satisfying cubes I’ve ever turned. After wiping away some of the factory lube and adding a little weight 5, mystic and fz calm, this is one of my favourite feeling cubes ever. Tbh I obky really notice the cheap plastic feel if I’m really trying to pay attention to it. M slices are amazing, it’s super quiet and soft feeling, and has that large internal radius feel akin to the ys3m (without actually having that big of an internal radius, I guess just different piece design). But yeah, for the price I absolutely recommend this over your other “budget” core mag options ie. super rs3m BC or moretry tianma. The core mags don’t auto align but they add needed stability to balance out the flimsiness (and they’re aftually noticeable unlike the invisible magnet strength of the rs3m super). Great cube. Just does have some downsides and not mainworthy for me over my current main (wrm v9), but still very enjoyable to solve and perfect for solving in public (iz so quiet).

Before I decided to take the plunge and order myself the dreaded Bagua cube, I’d read many reviews and knew full well what I was getting myself into. I knew about it catching and falling apart for just about every single person who’d written or talked about it online. Nonetheless, I was spellbound by the beautiful complexity (or perhaps complex beauty?) of the stickerless version in particular when thoroughly scrambled and shapeshifted. It’s been in my personal wishlist of expensive and elaborate cubes that I wanted to eventually get when I could justify the cost since I first saw/ heard about it. When it arrived, I was overjoyed, but cautious. I tested its turning carefully, but soon started scrambling it without further ado. Shortly after breaking it in a bit, I found it’s turning to be catchy at points (especially on the 45 degree turns) but otherwise surprisingly good. Within the first day of having it though (that night after coming home from work eager to play with it), I got cocky and forced a turn that I shouldn’t have. Believe what everyone says when they warn of explosive self-destruction – the darn thing dissolved into (many) pieces before my eyes; there was no hope whatsoever of replacing a piece or two and continuing on business as usual. And let me tell you, as everyone else will or has, putting the thing back together is a CHORE, and you will get frustrated. It took giving up on it after several hours, going to bed angry, and returning with bitter persistence the next day (plus a LOT of tape) to finally get the thing back together again. Before doing so completely though, I made sure to add a reasonable amount of lube and adjust the spring tensions (toward the tighter side) in the hopes of preventing it or at least forestalling any future explosive mishaps. After doing so, I watched Grumpy Old Cuber (?)’s YouTube video about adjusting it to minimize pops, which I strongly recommend watching before considering buying, as well as someone else’s (Red KB? Can’t remember tbh sorry) video about how to put it back together. Now, two things must be said at this point: 1) if you are considering getting the Bagua cube, make sure you know what you’re getting into and read and watch everything you can about it so when, not if it explodes, you are as prepared as you can be to deal with it accordingly; and 2) if you like complex cubes, challenging puzzles, beautiful/ artistic pieces for your personal collection, consider getting this cube. Many have said that the mf8 Sun cube is better/ more stable, and I can’t speak to that, but I’m sure it is. (I’d like to eventually get the Sun cube also.) So if you want a similar puzzle and don’t want to deal with the aforementioned issues, perhaps that’s a better option to contemplate. If those things don’t daunt you, and you’re like me and want a puzzle that is both amazing to play with and explore and is just totally amazing looking, then I think it is definitely worth it. The reconstruction process in itself is like a second puzzle experience for the price of one, lol.  

 P.S. I definitely have not solved this thing yet, and am okay with that for now. This is a very hard puzzle and took me a long time to find a solution. Before you scramble this, I would recommend that you set it up properly or you will have a very bad experience. I took off all of the center capes and wrapped the cube VERY tightly in tape and cut with an exacto knife a line between the top and middle layers and a hole to access the screw in the top layer. I then removed the top layer by unscrewing the screw from the core keeping every thing still wrapped tightly. I then added lots of dnm-37 but traxxas 50k would probably work as well along the tracks. I then put it back together and tighened each face by about a quarter of a turn and CAREFULLY removed the tape and loosened the cube until it could barely turn and then worked in the lube by doing 3x3 turns until it turned well.

BUT if you are not veeery careful when doing the turns, it will literally explode and melt in your hands. A pop means assembly from scratch, unscrew centers, use duct tape all over the place and so on. In no way should you take this puzzle in the train, for example, because the mess when it pops is truly massive. This can be mostly avoided by tightening the tensions in a balanced way.

review_title: Great puzzle if treated with love
review_text: This puzzle is a gem to have in your puzzle collection. If you want hours of tedious work, buy this puzzle. That being said, this puzzle must be treated with the utmost care; if you try to force a turn while shapeshifted, there is a good chance it will pop. You do not want to have to put this puzzle together, it is devilishly hard to put together; when assembling the puzzle, use masking tape or some other tape to keep pieces together. Tighten this puzzle down and go something like 1 or 2 turns counterclockwise to get a tolerable turning; also, lube the puzzle up, it will make it much more enjoyable.

This is a fantastic puzzle and is one of the most unique solving experiences I've had in a long time. It's a pricey puzzle, quite difficult, and is a bit unstable, but is worth the cost if you're looking for something to really sink your teeth in to. Not recommended to beginners or those who lack patience. Even once you get a handle on the solution it will take an hour or so to solve. I gave it a 4/5 rating, but the puzzle has many issues. It would have been a perfect score if it weren't for these issues, and similarly, I would have given the puzzle a much lower score (2 out of 5) if it weren't for it being so much fun to solve.  

  The puzzle is prone to popping due to the sheer number of pieces, and reassembly is a nightmare. Care must be taken to ensure alignment of the layer prior to turning. Reassembly is impossible without the use of some sort of masking tape to hold the pieces in place. The puzzle starts off very stiff and catchy, but if given enough love it will smooth out and loosen up. I recommend tightening the tensions down quite a bit and adding a bit of lubricant to help with stability. Also be aware that there tend to be slight imperfections in some of the thin edge pieces. It makes the pieces appear to be cracked, but doesn't appear to affect the durability of the puzzle. After multiple solves these "cracks" haven't spread at all. Seems to be a defect in the manufacturing process.

review_title: Fun cube but misleading picture - harder than it seems
review_text:
I got this puzzle along with the Earth version and solved earth pretty fast, but at this point I am at the last layer on this cube and haven't solved it yet. 

 People have said that Mars and Earth is about the same difficulty, but I think that Mars is a fair bit harder, I had to restart a couple of times as I realized I had started with the wrong layer and there isn't any layer suitable for last layer solving. 

 I thought it looked easy on the picture, but it only shows four sides of the six sides, so you don't get the entire layout. The blue side, which is NOT shown on the picture also has a triangle on it's side with two normal sides and one angled side facing the red and yellow layer.  

 I also found that you can never turn the green side because of this layout, where you can't turn white and yellow simultaneously without turning the blue side, and you can't turn the blue side while leaving the green side free to turn. Therefore this puzzle is harder than it seems, and I haven't solved it yet

Ootb it is very dry and you should still open it up and lightly lube (I used traxxas 50k) the inner faces of the black casing to get it moving well. I also didn't see a need to trim springs as I've had to do with LingAo; the excess spring is bent upwards on each end and they all moved very smoothly with no catching.
