review_title: Great puzzle and totally worth the money
review_text:
Although this is my first 5×5, and it has exceeded my expectations in every way. From my very first solves, the cube felt smooth, stable, and surprisingly forgiving, with very few lockups even during faster turning. 
       After making a few small setup adjustments (slightly loosening the compression and adding a balanced lube setup), the cube became even better. It has a stable, controllable feel while still being quick enough for fast solves. The UV coating is also fantastic—it provides a secure grip without feeling sticky and gives the cube a premium finish.
      If you're looking for a flagship 5×5, I genuinely think the GAN 5×5 is one of the best options available. It combines speed, stability, and smoothness better than any big cube I've tried. 
      My Secret Recommendation: Pair It with Hush 

 If you have access to FZ Hush, I highly recommend trying it in this cube. Hush doesn't dramatically change the speed, but it makes the cube noticeably quieter and gives it an incredibly smooth, refined feel. As the factory lube begins to wear in, adding a small amount of Hush (and optionally Silk if you enjoy an extra plush feel) makes the cube feel even more premium without sacrificing performance. 

 The result is a 5×5 that's: 

 Fast enough for competition.
 Stable during long solves.
 Exceptionally smooth.
 Surprisingly quiet. 

 Overall, the GAN 5×5 has exceeded my expectations. If you're considering upgrading to a flagship 5×5, I don't think you'll be disappointed. And if you're lucky enough to have a bottle of Hush, it's an excellent pairing that makes an already fantastic cube feel even better.

review_text:
For context, I mained the Dayan Nezha before getting the Gan 562.
  
 This cube just blew my expectations away. Both the outers and inners felt very stable and when solving, it just flowed more nicely. 3x3 stage has never felt easier, and there's just something about the inner layers that have me turning this cube everyday. It is addicting to turn, I've never been the type to solve a cube more than a 100 times in a day, but the first day I got this cube I went over 500 solves.

I even got my first sub 1:10 solve (1:08:xx) with this cube.  

 I'm also fairly certain that in 2 years, the Gan 562 won't have caps that fall off during solves, but we'll just have to wait and see. 

 Overall, it's a great cube!

 First of all, I would like to say that this cube is great, and right after getting it, I got multiple sub- 1:50s, which is good for me, and even a PB of 1:42. The outers on this cube are really smooth and have that buttery yet sandy but enjoyable GAN feel. They honestly feel like a 3x3.  The first issue I would like to address is inner layer lockups. When I corner cut on the outers, it cuts 45 degrees fine, which is crazy for a 5x5, however when I do the same with the inners, they go over each other and are locked in place, and every time I have to pull them apart, it feels like I will break a piece (I will attach a photo of this). Fortunately, the plastic seems to be very strong and I have not broken anything yet. 

 The second issue I will talk about is the cube box. It came broken, (again, I will attach a picture), and I really expect better on a $70 cube.  

 The final issue is that for some reason, the UV coating does not feel the same as other Gan cubes, I don't know if I got a bad batch, or if it is actually different.  

 Overall, this cube is an amazing 5x5, but it would be so much better if these issues were fixed. I don't want to pay $70 for a defective box and bad UV

Nothing about this cube is surprising except the price tbh. The biggest con I think it has is the center caps are pretty easy to remove, so they might fall off if you actually keep it on a keychain. The colors and texture of this cube matches Gan's other (current generation) cubes exactly 100%. The core mechanism is very traditional, with just screws and springs under the center caps. it's a bit difficult to get all the sides tensioned the same amount but it doesn't really matter... Corner cutting is surprisingly good but it doesn't feel very good or consistent while turning normally. It has a more traditional internal mechanism as well, instead of Gan's double-torpedo or whatever they call it. You can see in the pictures how the corners aren't as squared-off as Gan's other cubes, so corner twists are comparatively easier than other cubes, but still unlikely to happen. There's absolutely zero gap along the edges of the cube, where the different color stickerless faces meet together. And now I can technically brag I have the lightest speedcube on the market...... heh.

For a mini cube, it turns surprising well and is surprisingly well made with the intricate details of gan cubes and the honeycomb design on the inside. Obviously nobody is going to speedsolve this, but if you’re outside or in school (hopefully soon), it’s great to fidget around with, and frosted plastic makes it look very cool.

review_title: Best Megaminx on the Market (as of 2025)
review_text:
I typically write the downsides of a cube in my reviews and this cube is just perfect, I have no complaints. In my opinion, the DaYan Pro has inconsisent turning and the YuHu is too big, heavy, and has a weird colour scheme. Meanwhile, the MagLev on this cube doesn't makes it uncontrollable, it just makes the cube cleaner is a sense. The ballcore is feelable and does make a noticeable feeling of stability. The weight of this cube is super light considering the size of it which is probably due to the plastic quality of the cube. The only reason I could think of that some people might have issues with is colour scheme customization because the caps are hard to seperate and may damage the UV coating, but I find that to be a plus since now I don't need to worry about the caps seperating like on the YuHu. Lastly, the cube itself is just really pretty, having a cool looking adjustment system, the UV coating,  primary internals, and exposed magnets through magnet capsules. So despite being the most expensive, the features, durability, and performance of this cube 100% makes up for it and is a must buy if one wants to be competitive in Megaminx. And there is proof, it has set both WR single (22.89) and average (25.36) as of 2025.

I like my 15 more... A few people reading this just got so mad lmao. Apparently if you say evem the slightest thing negative about it people will explode with rage.  

 I had the same issue a lot of people had setting it up. Trying to adjust settings is like almost impossible.. There's no screw/bolt or literally anything holding the maglev in but a little T shape.. That holds two repelling magnets together...  Idk how else to quantify why I like my 15 more, but it just feels better to me. Caps are beyond annoying to me and this makes it easy. The 12 is also a lot more noisy. They both make noise, but the 12 definitely makes more. Small thing 

 Is the 15 worth the more money? Probably not.. But actually being able to change the settings is one HUGE reason I'd tell most people, especially beginners, that if they want a Gan, go for the 15 or have like the cubicle set it up or something. No matter how you cut it, you should be able to adjust settings without your cube exploding.... I still like it enough to not return it after it gave me a fn heart attack.....

review_title: Good cube, lives up to its name but it's expensive and only suits a specific turning style.
review_text:
This was the most recent of the "super popular flagships cubes" that I got. As you might know, many people say this is one of the best speedcubes ever made, and even though I was quite comfortable with the v9 and TV3 already, I wanted to get this one to try it out for myself and see if it was worth the praise. Out of the box it is, of course, way too fast, but it didn't take me too long to find settings that I was comfortable with. The adjustment tool looks kinda silly, but considering how good the cube is I can't complain, more on that later. As for the turning experience, at first I was not happy with it. This cube is very different from the v9/TV3, in that true to what people say about it, the GAN 12 demands accurate turning, and you can't force through misalignment like you can with other cubes. For the first few weeks I was constantly getting bad times due to lockups, and the solving experience was terrible. It was mostly because I was still used to the more lenient layer tolerances provided by the v9/TV3, but regardless I was initially disappointed with the cube. I knew that I was because of my poor turning though, so I kept solving with it to give it another chance. Eventually, my turning became more refined and accurate, and the cube rewarded that by being more smooth, reliable, and consistent. After a few months of solving I can get times that are on par to what I usually average.  

 As for how the cube itself, it feels very light and smooth to turn. Even with the strong core magnets, they don't feel overpowering thanks to the cube being so light. I noticed now the corner edge magnets feel weaker than those in other cubes that I have, although I'm not sure how much that contributes to the feel of the cube. The UV coating feels great, and even though the plastic pieces feel thin they don't feel fragile in the slightest; I've dropped this quite a few times with no issues, albeit onto carpet, so don't go dropping this onto the tiles of the kitchen floor. it does eat up lube very quickly; I recommend going for heavier lubes that are known to slow puzzles down. Use more than you usually would for other cubes, cause it breaks in after only about 100 solves or so. Oh, and I would also recommend cutting your nails before grinding solves, they can dig into the space between colored pieces and the primary pieces, and could damage them if you aren't careful.  

 Last but not least, the price is something to talk about. I got this when it was on a big sale, and if it wasn't for that I would've never bought this. It was definitely worth the purchase but at full price I would've been far more hesitant to make the investment. It's a great cube yes, but I agree with many others when they say there are better options in the market when cost is a consideration. Basically, if you can afford it, buy it. If not, get a WRM v9/10 or a TV3 or a v5 or basically any flagship under 50 USD. For it's age, the GAN 12 really has stood the test of time, but whether or not it'll still be viable in the future with the GAN 15/TV4/whatever other flagship on the horizon is up for debate. Time will tell, I suppose. I would recommend this cube, but only if you can afford it and only if you know you can adjust your turning style to match the cube.  

 TL;DR
 Great cube, lightweight, very satisfying to turn. Only works well if you can turn accurately. Locky, punishing and disappointing if you have poor turning accuracy. Very satisfying, highly rewarding, and incredibly smooth if you do have accurate turning. The price is pretty high but when on sale I'd recommend buying this.
With cubicle pro setup/lube it’s my instant main. By far the best cube I’ve had.

review_title: I'm not a bot when I say this cube is INCREDIBLE.
review_text:
Man, it's been a lot of history with this cube. 5.01, 4.86, 4.75, 4.69, 4.48. This thing has been through the world and back. But, despite its hype and the release of GAN cubes after this, my GAN 12 (affectionately named Tymon, yes I name my cubes, don't judge me, my dog smells and says nothing) stays strong. 

 You've all seen videos of unboxing and adjustment. I won't subject you through all that.  

 The performance is incredible as always. Out of the box, I guarantee you that IT WILL POP. It does not perform well without lube, just like your mo- 

 Adjustment is easy. My blue thing is set to 2, my clear thing is set to 3, and I use hexagonal magnets on the strongest setting, which still provides a smooth guiding feel without the CLUNK of the WRM V9.  

 Incidentally, I picked this cube over the V9 for that very reason. The beautiful quality of this cube is that regardless of how strong you set the magnets, it's never clicky. It flows incredibly well, and when turning fast, the magnets are not noticeable in feel but always helping stability. 

 Since this cube is too similar to the 11 and 13 onward, I'll be comparing it to my XS. 

 It's crunchier and not as quiet, but with my preferred lube setup (Compound X, DNM, and Mystic) it becomes nearly as quiet as my XS when they are setup identically. 

 They both cut very well, but the 12 feels more stable in small corner cuts than the XS, mostly due to the light weight and the loooooong core magnets. Notably, the XS suffers more than the 12 at very high angles, but who's cutting over 45 in a regular solve?  

 The 12 feels similar to the XS in the fact that it feels like you are turning absolutely nothing. They are both light, fast, and smooth, with no hint of resistance or sandiness. Of course, lube will change this, but it's worth noting. 

 The color shades are of course perfect, and the UV coating is VERY helpful with my hands being perpetually dry (I swear, my hands eat more Vaseline than a 2007-era Rubik's brand.) My only gripe is the lack of a stickered version still available, but hey, I own an SM, so that's cool. (I'm not selling it. EVER.) 

 The only downsides are the fact that it's pretty hard to get the setup right and that it's more prone to pops than the XS. For the setup, just follow my instructions and you should be okay, and the pops are negligible, but I feel as if I just needed to say something at least a little negative so I don't feel like I'm blowing hot air. 

 Bottom line? Better than the 11. Better than the 13. Better than the 14. Better than the V9. I love it. 

 (BTW, 45,000th review!)

review_title: Absolutely the best of the best, however it didn't make it to "MAIN" status...
review_text:
I bought this cube because I got a GAN 11 for free during a sale here at TheCubicle, and I thought, if the GAN 11 is this good, the GAN 12 Maglev must be better since it doesn't use springs, and has core to corner magnets... 

 So I pulled the trigger and bought the 12 Maglev UV, and I absolutely love it!!! As usual, the price was great (it was on sale) and the shipping was within 3 business days to Canada. 

 It feels great, looks great, and even sounds great (once lubed properly). I see some reviewers saying it feels and sounds cheap, however you have to remember that it's extremely light weight, which means there's lots of free space inside, causing the sound to reverb. Once you lube the cube, then that sound goes away. There's no spring sound, because there aren't any. It's also very fast, combine that with being lightweight, you'll get a lot of noise if it's dry, I like to use DNM-37, then a little bit of a gummy lube to slow it down just a bit. 

 After that, it turns really well... I love this cube, I can see why it's the "best of the best", however my Weilong Maglev (purple edition) is my main cube, however I'm a bit biased towards purple cubes, although it does feel awesome... The GAN 12 would easily become my main, however it doesn't look the part... If they came out with another special edition like the Peacock (green) edition, but with different colors, then that could easily become my main as it performs just as well as the Weilong Maglev. 

 Not to mention, adjusting the magnets is REALLY easy, and the core to corner magnets are easily replaceable... and the mini airpod box is a nice touch to store the extra parts for the GAN 12... 

 All in all, it's a great cube if you're willing to spend the money. However if you don't want to spend this amount of money, then going with the Weilong Maglev would be your next best choice, in my opinion...

review_title: What I've been looking for in a smart cube
review_text: I'm so happy with this. Best bluetooth cube I've ever had.

I have a GAN 12 UI Smart cube and a GAN 16 Max as well. This GAN i4  smart cube is as good or better, with a much better price than either of those.  

 What this cube is: Is a GAN 16 Max ($85) with a smart ball core added. The pieces are identical with minor changes to accommodate adding the smart ball core. The edge pieces have larger magnets but the edge flanges have the tiny magnets removed.  

 The corner pieces also have larger magnets. The replaceable magnet stalks on the 16 M are no longer needed to reach the core, and the i4 has them replaced with shorter, fixed-in-place, magnets. The end result is a cube with a much stronger locked-in magnetic system, but still retaining the flagship speed and turning of the 16 Max.  

 The tension system is pure GAN 16 Max. Nothing has changed and you can likely trade parts with the GAN 16. Matter of fact, if you remove the magnet stalks, you can likely interchange all the pieces except the core between the 16 Max and i4 cubes. I think it would work, though you would loose the magnetic tune GAN has setup.  

 And they did all this for $15 less, and threw in the charging pod as well for free. I got nothing negative to say. You could choose this over both the 16 Max and the 12ui and you would not be wrong to do so.  

 I might even say this is the best Smart Cube money can buy right now.

review_title: THIS is the cube for a blind solver (and it's gorgeous if you can see it!)
review_text:
If you can see the sparkly purple on this cube, it looks _amazing_, it just does, the pictures cannot do it justice. 

 I dunno if I'd ever try to do CFOP on this thing (I'm a n00b who just started learning CFOP), but I can solve this thing with my eyes closed using the standard beginner methods, sort of. One reviewer said they used the color stickers as kinda training wheels. My advice? Skip 'em. If you know the beginner alg, you won't need them within five minutes. 

 The trick is is to take advantage of the hub pieces to check that things are flush. Use the longest center (opposite the logo which is the shortest) to create a cross on the bottom, ignoring sides. Rotate the pieces up, turn the top to find the side that's flush with the "white" edge pointing up, and rotate it down when you do. 

 From there F1L and F2L follow beginner method strategies: If an edge in the top layer matches a center's thickness, it is either a skinny LL piece, or it needs to be dropped to the left or the right. Basic beginner method stuff. For LL, the same thing. 

 Now, learning these algs on a mirror block if you're blind might be more work. I suggest skipping the cubing notation while getting the hang of manipulating the mirror block—it's a lot to keep track of and it doubles the work of memorizing the algorithm. 

 For example, for dropping an edge left or right for F2L, the first move is to "push away" the edge from the side it's going to, regardless of whether it be right or left. That's true regardless of right-handed or left-handed mirrors of the algorithm. Reduce the cognitive load! 

 No, the place to learn cubing notation IMO is doing scrambles. The more scrambles you do, the more instinctive the notation will become. Then you can start thinking about the notation for what you're doing. Baby steps. 

 Whether you're sighted or blind, YOU can do a mirror block!

review_title: Basically the GAN14 Pro and the Weilong v11 combined
review_text:
I had a chance to try this cube at GAN's offline Shanghai store, and you can view my video review below as well for an in-depth look at the puzzle. 

 This cube is the combination of the GAN14 Pro and the Super Weilong v2 / Weilong v11. It retains GAN's signature hard plastic, giving it a very clacky and tactile feel, similar to GAN's more recent 3x3s. This feeling is the most apparent on the 14 Pro and 14. However, this cube also has the nice rounded feeling that comes from the cuts, otherwise described as "bubbly", similar to MoYu's recent Weilong piece designs.  

 The cube is very lubed out-of-the-box, and you can feel the cube breaking in. However, the lube that they use is quite light and breaks in very quickly, leaving you with an extremely fast puzzle. The demo cube at Shanghai was completely dry (likely due to the amount of turns that cube experiences daily, being a demo cube), and you can see how ridiculously low-friction that cube was by going to the timestamp 9:48 in the video below. If you want the cube to be more controllable, I'd suggest using some heavier lube (I like to use XMT10 to retain a faster feel, but Phil from TheCubicle recommends Super Honey for heavier turners) and a higher maglev tension setting (the default is setting 8 out of 12 total settings, and I use setting 11). 

 The cube has pretty good corner-cutting, better than any of GAN's recent flagships, however I still wouldn't classify this cube as forgiving in any way. It is still a modern GANCUBE, after all. If you don't have light or accurate turning, you won't have a good time with this cube. On the other hand, if you perform well with modern GANs but enjoy the newer Weilong's feel, then this cube is perfect for you. 

 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 

 Some things that might be interesting to hardware nerds out there:
 1. The edge-core magnet is removable, it is not interchangable (meaning there are no replacement magnets of a different strength for the edge-core). You can remove it just like you do with the corner-core magnets, using the same "fire-hydrant" tool. Removing the edge-core magnet reduces the severity of auto-align. (The magnet is a bit finnicky to remove, so be careful) 

 2. The adjustment system is held together with a screw. This screw is NOT for adjusting axis distance, and you SHOULD NOT touch it. If you go to 7:53 in the video below, you'll see a cross-section of the core, and the screw only goes through the top bit of the core. This indicates that the only real purpose of having the screw there is to replicate the little cross on the top of older GAN cores which holds the GES together and in place. If you tighten or loosen the screw, the adjustment system will be more difficult to adjust and the cube will lock up, or the adjustment system will start adjusting itself and the centers will pop out, respectively. 

 3. Just something minor I've noticed, but a good side-effect of using a screw instead of a cross to hold the GES in place is that, when adjusting axis distance, you can press down with the tool and turn the opposite way without removing the whole GES. This can help save a bit of time and effort when increasing the axis distance one-by-one (for example, when adjusting from 4 -> 5 you can do it directly by going backwards, instead of going forwards: 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 6 -> 5). This does not work with maglev tension though, so you still have to adjust that normally.

review_title: Gan 12 Maglev Review and my setup
review_text:

 Center-Distance travel (blue ring on top with numbers)
 -setting 5 

 Tension ( the thing that the three long prong-like things on the tool adjust)
 -Setting 4 

 Magnet rod adjustment
 -hexagonal rods with the adjustment thing in the middle 

 Lubes
 -take 2 opposite edge peices out and apply SILK lubricant to the tracks of each (dont be afraid to overdo it)
 then break the lube in with a few solves
 -Then apply Lubicle Speedy to opposite corner and edge peices, not on the tracks, idk what they are called but apply it to the faces of the peices that make contact with any other part of the cube. 

 Do about 100 solves and this cube will blow your mind! 

 The cube could benefit from corner cutting a little but it is made up with the auto-aligning Technology)

review_title: Best 11x11 on the Market (but not perfect)
review_text:
This puzzle turns pretty decently out of the box, and even better after a few solves and lots of lube (I used DNM-37). 
 The size of this cube is great. It's small enough to where algorithms are possible through muscle memory (though I do have slightly larger hands). This small size also means it's not necessary to table the cube to keep layers in alignment. It's also light and not too straining on the hands during a full solve. 
 The magnets also help a bit with layer alignment, though they do not eliminate misalignments & locking completely. This puzzle is really a competitive, main-worthy option. 

 The feel of this cube is slightly bumpy but very smooth, with a hint of a sandy feel to it. It's pretty quiet (just slightly louder than the GAN 356 X). The feel is also more tactile and less smooth than the X, but I like it so far. Execution of algorithms flows very nicely, and the stronger magnet options in this cube really keep it stable. The customization is great, and it's semi-easy to understand after you read the provided pamphlet.  

 That being said, the customization provides a lot of options, but they are not the options I would have liked to see. I enjoy slower, more stable cubes, but the customization options essentially range from "fast" to "really fast" and from "moderately stable" to "unstable." This cube is pretty fast on the most conservative settings (the default settings out of the box), and so you will need to rely on lube to slow it down. I am satisfied, however, with the magnet options, which range nicely from "weak" to "pretty strong," and you can change them simply by sliding a wheel around on each edge piece. I would also say be aware of the shades on this cube. The stickerless version sports full-bright shades, which means the red is borderline fluorescent. Not a big deal. It looks nice, but I wasn't expecting it after looking at the pictures. 

 So overall, this is a great cube, and I'd definitely recommend giving it a try. The feel is similar to the X but distinctly unique, and the performance is just as good (if not better).

The performance of the cube is good. 
 However, there're a few cons the cube has that I want to address:  

 - The center caps are way too tight, or at least I can not open any center cap by hand without tools. So I had to use the screwdriver to pry the center caps. And when I tried to open the blue center cap, the screwdriver glided a bit and left a scratch on the surface. So even though I love cubes so much, I didn't feel sorry for my Tengyun V2 because I was just glad that I didn't hurt my fingers.  

 - The numbers printed on the elasticities and tensions' adjustment system are almost illegible to me, especially on the blue side. I had to use magnifier to adjust them. 

 - The description of the adjustment system on the pamphlet is confusing. I understand the concept of the center piece travel control and the tension control are different, and in this cube, they both can be adjusted with the same tool on the same parts. However, I think it would be much better to say, "Use the adjustment tool to press and twist the **tension control** until the arrow aligns the correct number of the control set", than what it is now on the pamphlet.  

 - Besides, if you did not press down the adjustment control system enough, you would be adjusting the screw depth directly from loose/tightening the screw itself. So, pressing down the adjustment control system before twisting it is important. And I believe it would be helpful if they put an extra warning about it on the pamphlet.  

 - The longest axis distance that could be set by the center piece travel control system is still too tight for me. I ended up just using the screwdriver to adjust it. So, won't it be much better to let the control system cover a wider axis distance range? Otherwise, what is the point of having the adjustment system of the axis distance if the customer can adjust it easier with a screwdriver than the adjustment tool? 

 - The spring noise out of the box was crazy. I know it's normal for a cube to have some spring noise, and I eliminated the noise by adding some silicone lube to the spring. But considering this should be a flagship cube based on its price and the struggle of opening the center caps, it's just an awful first impression the cube gave me.  

 - This one is probably not a problem to other cubers, but it's a problem to me. The cube felt pretty sandy out of the box, and it's much sandier than the Tengyun V1 M. And even though it had tons of factory lube, it still reminded me of some dry Moyu Meilong more than any other Dayan cubes.  

 In conclusion, as an old cuber who had been a fan of Dayan cubes, I am ultimately disappointed by Dayan Tengyun V2 M. I hope they can make a better and unique release next time.

I went on a buying spree here at thecubicle (always fun) and this was one of the cubes I picked up. You have to take some time and mess with the settings, there are a lot...but if you approach it with some patience and time you will be very happy with where it ends up. I'm very happy with the cube and would definitely recommend that people should check it out.

TL;DR: This cube is a great value for $32, but there are some issues that might stop top speedcubers from maining it. 

 My settings: medium magnets, 0.6 tensioning, 1.0 spring compression. 

 Let's start with the pros first. The turning retains the same quiet and swooshy feeling that the original Tengyun was popular for. However, I have noticed that this cube is a little louder than the original.  The cube can also be setup to be very stable or very flexible, which is important since the instability of the original Tengyun was a let down for me.  

 Next, the customization system. I think this magnet system is one of the most straightforward systems on a cube today.  The magnets can be easily changed and takes very little time. The spring system isn't ideal however. I much prefer the Gan and Moyu systems, as they are more simplistic. In the Tengyun v2, there are 2 ways to adjust tensions, the screw and the smaller blue ring. This makes the smaller blue ring completely pointless, which just complicates an already complicated system. Even on my moderate-ish settings, this cube is very stable and controllable, which is definitely a pro.  

 However, this stability leads to some corner cutting issues, which is probably the biggest reason most pros wouldn't use this cube as their main. Small corner cuts, especially reverse cuts, take a lot more effort than nearly every cube on the market. This leads me to have to slow down my turning during solves, especially during last layer, which leaves me getting inconsistent results. When I get a short last layer, I get solves that are much faster than what I average, and I've even set a PB of 4.14 on this cube. However, many times when I get a more complicated last layer, the catching and locking from the lackluster corner cutting leads me to get several 10s and high 9s. (For context, I average high 7 on my Gan XS).  

 Another issue I've run into is the increased weight. Although it is only 83g, other brands like Gan and Qiyi are pushing the weight of their cubes down and down, and the Tengyun v2 is one of the first cubes in years where the weight increased over the past generation. 

 However, the corner cutting problem would likely only affect faster speedsolvers, and I think the satisfying smooth feeling and the high amount of customization would make it very compelling for newer and intermediate cubers looking for an upgrade. And for $32, there's no other cube that offers this level of customization and performance. However, if customization isn't your first priority, you might have better luck trying out the Gan 356 M, which offers better performance at the same price. Even though this cube is a drastic upgrade over the Tengyun v1, it still has a bit to go to compete with other flagships like the Gan XS, Valk Elite, and WR M.

I used the TengYun V2 and then V3 as my main for a very long time. Just switched to the GuHong. I like the very light turning effort and the magnet strength is pretty much just right for accurate turns. Maybe my Tengyuns were just worn out or something, but I felt like I was fighting with them anymore. They were a lot of work to use. The GuHong is so light and easy, I can cube a lot without tiring out my hands. Only complaint (costing them a star) is the white center cap logo: it's fused on (not just a logo sticker) so the cube is not comp legal for 3-blind. That's a real shame.

After one day out of the box, I've had time to do a few solves and run some last layer practice. This is a Dayan so unboxing it is a sloppy affair; the cube has to be cleaned with a fresh napkin from all the factory Lube before using. 

 Dayan's new packaging is THE BEST among all brands. I don't think there are ANY accessories except for a couple of small brochures, and this is a great thing. The box itself is attractive and compact and has a magnetic clasp, with a sturdy foam liner (I would like to see a multi-compartment rigid case designed with exactly these features.) I am going to keep this box; I usually get rid of Gan and Moyu boxes/accessories. 

 The cube itself has the best tribology of any in my collection. Yes, I deployed "tribology". Can someone in the class describe what I mean by "tribology"? Hint: in cubing, its important. (The cube with the worst tribology is the X-Man V3.) 

 I have the 55 mm Maglev version. The turning and stability are noticeably different compared with my Guhong 54 Standard. I think its actually better, but this is one of those things that's down to personal preference. 

 I noticed incredible layer stability on slice algs, but I get too loose on wide-U G-perms. I think the magnets are on the weak side, and there's no adjustment (not that I really make use of this on, say, the Tengyun.) All in all, a very very good cube so far. 

 I wish Dayan sold their lube. I think the cube design is probably sensitive to the lubricant, and once you use something besides the factory stuff, a little bit of the Dayan magic goes away. But wow, what a puzzle. they don't get much better (if at all.)

 In conclusion, you should get this or the standard if you want a cheap, good speedcube.

The only flaw with this cube is that it barely reverse corner cuts, reaching at best a quarter of a piece, and it appears that external catching between the centre and corner pieces is the cause. A Florian mod is likely to be able to fix this. Forward corner cutting on the other hand, is a full piece which is nothing special. In my opinion, this outperforms all the other ShengShou 4x4s as well as all other 4x4s in it's price range. review_title: Not as good as I hoped
review_text:
I own an X-Man Galaxy 2 Megaminx, which proves that the dodecahedron shape can move incredibly well. I also own a Yuxin 9x9, which shows that super large, non-WCA puzzles can have a well engineered mechanism. I was hoping the ShengShou Gigaminx would be a merger of those two qualities, but unfortunately it's just not. 

 Even after I loosened tensions, I still found this Gigaminx required careful hand positioning and full two hand grip to get faces rotated. Even then I found myself catching against the interior pieces often. I took my time and didn't try to speed solve it, since I enjoy casually solving large puzzles with music or TV, but even then I felt like I was getting uncomfortably close to a pop. 

 This is also just personal preference, but personally I feel like the color scheme is just muted and ugly, and especially does not age well next to the rest of my collection. I got mine in black to help with color identification. If I was to order again, I would get it in white instead to help make the cube feel a little brighter. 

 If you love collecting all sorts of puzzles like I do, there aren't that many gigaminxes on the market, so this is a good option in that regard. But if you're also like me in that you enjoy a pleasant solve, you might find yourself leaving this one on the shelf after a couple solves.

review_title: High quality feel but locks up
review_text:
First kilominx, so I have nothing to compare it to. In general I am very happy with it.  

 This puzzle has a high quality feel and is great in most areas, but it tends to lock up. I think it is because when you hold it with your left hand, you are holding the faces of corner pieces that can move rather than holding the fixed center pieces like a megaminx. This results in the core shifting under the pieces you are holding, and it tends to lock up.   

 That said, I really enjoy solving it. The big stickers make it look awesome, and it's a fun challenge to try to solve it quickly.  It has a quality feel consistent with other "just below flagship" puzzles I own.

It turns pretty good at has decent corner cutting. It is slightly slow but thats ok for me because I am not a megeminx speedsolver. The one problem aI have is that the reverse corner cutting is terrible. If you try a tperm or other alg the has an f move you will probably be confused by why the layer wont turn. 

 So it is definitely a good cube that I recommend to people if you want a fun puzzle to solve and if you want to get into megaminx, just don't expect to be able to reverse corner cut.

Turns well, really smooth. Came practically covered in lube on one side, like it was applied during packaging and just... all leaked out... but I wiped it up and it's dried some now, so it's all good. Still had plenty in it. Sticker shades look nice, and stickers seem to be pretty high quality; my boyfriend has one as well that he's had for several years and the puzzle itself and the stickers on it don't seem to be suffering too much either.  

 This is a very fun puzzle to solve, which is only added to by how satisfying it is to turn. It's like a 2x2 for a megaminx. If you know 2x2/3x3 you should be able to figure out all but last layer intuitively, maybe that too.

review_title: Well built and turns well, but solving is tedious
review_text:
This is a well built puzzle, and turns very well, especially for a dodecahedron. However, I was hoping for a greater challenge, but it's essentially a more tedious 4x4.  

 I personally find solving a 6x6x6 or 7x7x7 cube more enjoyable, and if you don't have one of those, I'd recommend going that direction before going for a dodecahedron.  

 Like all ShengShou cubes, this comes out of the box a little greasy due to the excess of lube (very thin) lube, which a gentle rub down with a kitchen towel will take care of. I added just a pinch of Traxxas 50K to the inside, which is probably unnecessary, but is my personal preference. 

 One thing I did like about learning to solve the Dodecahedron, its it helped me understand the generalities of cube algorithms -- which is just good nerdy fun. But that said, this will probably never be one of my main (daily) cubes (puzzles).

review_title: Flawless, a real work of art
review_text:
This puzzle is absolutely stunning, a true work of art, and instantly the pride of my collection. Not only does it look impressive in its immensity and complexity, but its performance is incredible. 

 First off, the puzzle is gigantic, much larger than I expected. The Shengshou Teraminx looks comical compared to it. Although it is both bulky and heavy, its true dodecahedral structure makes it much more comfortable to manipulate than the MF8 version. Right out of the box it turns effortlessly. The tensions and lubrication seem to have been carefully calibrated to provide an enjoyable experience, and I had to contribute no additional changes to the way it turns. It's simply perfect as it comes.  

 I know this puzzle is a lot of money, but in my opinion, it is truly a must have for any collector or puzzle enthusiast. I cannot tell you enough how much I absolutely adore this puzzle. I will surely spend hours on this in the coming weeks and months.

If you like big minx-type puzzles, this is the one. Out of the box I thought the turning was very stiff and that the Teraminx was much better, but after 1 solve, the turning improved drastically. A puzzle this size needs to be broken in, but the turning improves with use without lube or adjusting tension. A very sturdy and impressive puzzle, I’d highly recommend it.

To conclude, the Shengshou Petaminx is an incredible puzzle with great turning! I hope that a stickerless variant of the puzzle could be made as well! I recommend this puzzle to anyone who has some dough to spend and who likes to solve long and tedious puzzles :)

 A fun and surprising challenge!  Recommended for any collection!

This is a great cube. After lots of DNM37 and tension adjustment, it's very smooth and stable. I don't get lockups, but I'm very slow so your results may be different if you're fast. I use my own method which uses lots of slice moves, and this cube makes them almost effortless. It's a direct solving method, so I don't use a 3x3 stage, and I can't speak to this cube's feeling for reduction solves. 

 It's not as good as my Aosu GTS2 but I use it more because I love the classic stickered look and the magnetic feel. Compared to the Qiyi mini Thunderclap, it's a whole lot smoother and lighter - I recommend the Mr. M over the Thunderclap 100%. 

 Adjusting the tensions was difficult. There is a very narrow range that works. Initially I loosened it, but that caused lockups, so I tightened it a half turn tighter than stock tensions - and the cube would not move at all. It was literally impossible to turn. So, I put it back to approximately stock tensions and corrected some uneven sides, and then it started to feel very good. So, I suggest sticking close to stock tensions but taking care to tension evenly. A whole lot of fast lube also helps.

Would you believe that this thing took me a full half hour to solve? It's deceptively difficult, as the 5 axes result in situations that you wouldn't encounter on a standard 1x3x3 four sided puzzle. If that wasn't bad enough, the "ghost" nature of it constantly makes you end up placing pieces where they don't actually belong, and being all one single color means that you can't tell when looking at a piece which of the 10 combinations of position/orientation it should go in for a corner piece, or which of the two orientations it should go in for an edge piece (ok, that's a slight lie because the "brushed metal" design of the stickers make the edge orientations obvious, though one edge _almost_ looks correct when it's oriented wrong). By my math, this puzzle has over 60,000 possible piece arrangements (and given the odd number of sides, I don't think there is much in the way of parity to make the number of possible scrambles that much lower). So in the end you have a little puzzle that is great to fidget with, takes actual effort to solve, and slips effortlessly into a pocket. 

 Ok, enough about the difficulty. What about the puzzle quality? Well, the pieces rattle a little, but still feel solid enough when you turn them. It can corner cut ever so slightly, but not enough that you won't run into lockups from time to time. Due to the trapezoidal shape of the edge pieces, you can't make any quarter turns of two sides and then turn the edge in between them much like you can on a normal floppy cube (technically you could force this move, but it's clear the puzzle isn't meant to move in this way, and I believe if you did this you'd make the puzzle "unsolvable" without repeating the action). The only downside is that it's stickered, and as such it's going to have a limited lifespan if you keep it in your bag or pocket (though in theory you could remove all the stickers and it'd be just as solvable, and in fact even a little harder due to the lack of clues as to edge orientation).

 (at least that's my theory)   

 so, in my opinion its not bad, but it has a few issues that are really frustrating 

 1. constant catches, way more then any of the other cubes i own
 2. the tiles fly off sometimes if you try to push through some of the lockups, and can be quite tricky to retrieve
 3. it needs a lot of lube or the plastic kinda sticks to itself a little and a few more not worth mentioning  

 i do, however, really like the feel of it when its set up, its very smooth and very buttery, and when it doesn't lock up, its an absolute joy to solve. and as far as magnets go, they are a little on the light side, but i honestly prefer weaker magnets to their stronger counterparts. 

 so would i recommend it?
 well, that would depend, if you're looking for a new main, this ain't it, you can get much better for much less (cough cough, little magic)
 but if you're just looking for a a new cube with a different feel, don't mind paying 18$ and are averaging around 20 seconds or more (give or take) then yeah, i'd say go ahead.

 •Corners cuts about 45°, does have some lock up spots

review_title: YJ YuLong V2 M vs. MoYu RS3 M 2020 vs. DaYan GuHong V4 M
review_text:
A review of a nice sample of budget cubes, current prices $7.99, $9.99 (w/magnet kit), and $14.99 respectively. 

 After adjusting and lubing to my preferred state, here are my observations: 

 Corner cutting:  Almost identical, the DaYan may have a TINY bit more reverse corner cutting. 

 Speed:  YJ slowest, DaYan fastest, but your lube can change that somewhat. 

 Weight:  YJ 88 grams, MoYu 87 grams, DaYan 65 grams. 

 Color:  DaYan colors are slightly more saturated, except the yellow looks more orange compared to the other two, and the white is a cool white and the other two use a 
              warm white. 

 Sound:  MoYu may be the loudest, but not by much.  It has more spring noise.  DaYan is the quietest. 

 Feel:  YJ has the best quality "feel" (subjective, of course).  MoYu finish is frosted, but it becomes smooth before long. 

 Magnets:  DaYan seems to be the strongest, the other two less so. 

 Miscellaneous:  MoYu pieces will separate a bit along the edges occasionally, but it's very little and not a detriment.
 		             MoYu has an adjustment system, but it's used so infrequently it's of no consideration, unless it's important to you to have it.
 		             DaYan cube faces show the most sink from the reinforcing ribs (molding issue).  If the face thickness was increased or the pack and hold times in the 
                                          injection molding process were optimized, it would improve the appearance.  But it makes no difference in performance.
 		            YJ corner twists the easiest, though if you tighten it a bit it isn't a big problem.  The other two are quite good at not twisting. 

 Conclusion:  First of all, the best speedcubers could sub 10 on any of these all day every day, that's how good these cubes are.
 	                However, they're freaks, so most people won't be able to do that.
 	                The typical person will be held back more by his technique than by his choice of cube, and if you are sub 15, any of these cubes should be fine.
 	                However, once you improve your technique as much as you can within genetic and practice time limitations, your cube can help you eke out that last little bit 
                                  of time you're looking for.
 	                And perhaps around the 10 second mark or so you may be ready to try something a bit more expensive to see if it'll help.
 	                Of course you may always be able to improve you time by getting a more expensive cube earlier, but if you're reading this you're looking for a budget cube 
                                  anyway, and any of these will suffice for a long time.  Trust me, for the most part your cube isn't holding you back -- if you have one as good as one of 
                                  these. 

 Preferences:  YJ feels the best in your hand, but the MoYu is only 25% more expensive and you get fewer corner twists.
 	                 If you like fast and crisp turning and snappy magnets, the DaYan is quite nice at 90% more expensive than the YJ. 

 Recommendation:  Really none of these are bad and we're splitting hairs to rank them, but here goes:
 		                     YJ is the budget pick
 		                     MoYu is the best buy
 		                     DaYan is the best overall.

review_title: Yupo V2 M: Great budget option with some minor flaws
review_text:
The YJ Yupo V2 M is without a doubt one of the better "budget" 2x2s out there. Definitely a great option for new cubers who are looking to get a magnetic 2x2 that won't break the bank. Performance wise, it delivers solid overall performance, but it's personally not my preference in terms of speed, feel and magnet strength.  

 I've seen some people claiming that they can barely feel the magnets which leads me to believe they received a faulty puzzle, because the magnets in this 2x2 are pretty damn strong. The magnet strength results in a "bumpy" feeling, which I'm not a huge fan of, as I find that it makes the puzzle feel sluggish and not as fluid when performing algorithms. Turning this 2x2 feels like it requires significantly more effort than other "budget" magnetic 2x2s, like the Yuxin Little Magic M and the QiYi MS. The corners also twist really easily, and due to the fact that the puzzle requires more effort to turn because of the strong magnets, I end up accidentally twisting corners quite frequently during solves which is really frustrating. 

 As for the positives, it corner cuts very well even out of the box on the stock tensions, and once broken in, has a very smooth feeling if you can tolerate the bumpiness caused by the magnets. The stickerless shades are also nice. 

 Overall, although it isn't my preferred 2x2, I still think that it's a great option for the price. If you're a beginner you definitely can't go wrong buying this puzzle. An overall solid effort by YJ for a budget magnetic 2x2.

review_title: Excellent 6x6! The best budget 6x6! It’s my Main!
review_text: Well first of, I have to give a praise to YJ for producing amazing magnetic cubes for an economical price. I haven’t heard that many reviews on this cube though. But from what I’ve heard, it’s really great. CoachTabe mained this cube I believe until the MGC 6x6 came out. Talking about the cube, it’s layers have a pretty consistent speed and the inner most is very fast. The magnets can be felt in all the layers but they are quite light to medium. Out of the box, the tensions very loose and the cube was locking up. If you turn the screws from 180° to 360°, the cube feels the same except it is much less prone to popping and locking. An issue with the MGC was that midges would pop a lot, but the midges on this cube don’t at all. I haven’t got a lock up or a pop on the Yushi and it is so fast. It is more stable and smoother than the Little Magic M. Corner cutting is good (that isn’t important on big cubes)I love this cube so much. There is only a minor problem with this cube and it catches. The catches are not that noticeable compared to other 6x6’s. I don’t care if it’s cheap but I can probably say this is the 2nd best 6x6 after the MGC. It’s only a $9 difference between the MGC and this. This magnetic budget 6x6 is cheaper than some of the non magnetic ones and it performs way better. The G6 is just so bad. I highly recommend the Yushi V2, if you like a fast and very stable 6x6) Get it! One thing I’m hoping for is a budget magnetic 8x8.

review_title: Great for the price, quick, loose, and surprisingly stable
review_text:
This is my second 6x6, and my first was a V-cube. Meaning this was a MASSIVE upgrade, and actually made solving 6x6 fun for me again! As far as the cube itself goes, I'm very happy with it. 
 It's got great turning, each layer turns well, slices are consistent and turn extremely well, even 3 layer slice moves are a breeze. 
 Color scheme is great, easy recognition even in low light. 
 Magnet strength is good, but I could use a touch more strength on the inner layers and a touch less on the outer layer. 
 Feel is super sandy at first, but after a few solves, it smooths out nicely, and becomes pretty fluid and quick moderately quickly.
 Speed is real with this cube. It's possibly not your competition cube for elite level solvers, but for people like me who solve in the ~8min range, it's more speed than I could use.
 Stability surprised me the most with this cube. It feels pretty loose, especially compared to my MGC cubes, that I was worried about pops. (My yj 4x4 popped a lot until it was tightened a bunch.) I haven't adjusted the tension at all, and haven't had a single pop in 50 or so solves. I've had it lock up because of bad slice moves by me and always been able to just turn the cube back, undo the lockup instantly, and move on. I've thought it would pop several times, especially while it was breaking in Z but it just never seems to pop. I haven't had one, and I've done some truly terrible slices that should have netted me a pile of pieces and a core. 

 All in all, this is a great cube, especially at the price point.
 My 5x5 and 7x7 are both MGC's, and there is a notable difference it quality and feel. Some may prefer the lighter, looser feeling of this line of cubes, but I will say I much prefer the MGC's tight-but-speedy feel, texture and piece shape, and magnet strengths. For me, as much as this cube is fantastic and worth every penny and more, I'd spend the extra $10 for the MGC. The extra dopamine from how good those cubes feel to solve is worth it.

review_title: YJ MGC 7x7 vs Moyu Meilong Magnetic
review_text:
I am relatively new to speed solving larger cubes so take what I say with a grain of salt. My 3x3 PR is 21 seconds, and my 7x7 PR is down to 8:07 with about 100 total solves. The YJ MGC 7x7 is smooth and stable out of the box with strong and satisfying magnetic feel.  

 My first 7x7 was the Moyu Meilong Magnetic. My PR instantly dropped about a minute when I got the YJ MGC. It is slightly larger than the Moyu and I have larger/longer fingers which makes turning, especially during edge building, feel more accurate.  

 That being said the Moyu Meilong 7x7 is still an incredible cube and I would rate it just below the YJ MGC, maybe better if you have small hands.  

 I hadn’t had any pieces pop on the YJ for about 30 solves until I added some lube. This cube is so smooth out the box so maybe I added too much.  

 My only complaint is the sticker being placed slightly off center on the white side. The sticker on my YJ MGC 5x5 was also off center and started peeling instantly. It would be cool if they incorporated a permanent logo design into the cube itself because I like displaying what logo the cube is.  

 Overall the YJ MGC 7x7 is an amazing cube for the price and I plan on getting every cube in the lineup from 2x2-7x7.

review_title: A great sister cube to the YS3M.
review_text:
I wanted to preface this by saying it's an early review. It's not fully broken in yet, but I believe it has serious potential. 

 Anyway, a review. Unboxing is interesting, with a similar slide-out style to the box as the GAN 14. Accessories include some spare hardware, an indecipherable pamphlet, and the world's worst screwdriver that ALWAYS, ALWAYS breaks within the first thirty seconds. YJ YOU MAKE GREAT CUBES, WHY CAN'T YOU GET A SCREWDRIVER RIGHT???!!!! 

 Out of the box, the cube, to put it in the most polite words I can, was absolute unfettered garbage. It was too tight, bone dry, and had a feeling akin to scraping sandpaper on a toilet seat. The tensions were all wrong, and it was incredibly draggy. 

 Everything changed when I loosened a screw, and put a few drops of lube in. It instantly became fast, buttery-smooth, and as fluid as a blocky cube can be. Cuts are easy, despite a snapping feeling akin to newer, clackier cubes as opposed to my preferred smoother cuts, per GTS2M or MF3RS2M. The feeling was blocky, yes, but not in a cheap way. It felt like an alternate-universe YS3M, despite being much cheaper. 

 When looking at the hardware, the similarities continue. Like the YS3M, the core magnets are not too strong but still noticeable, and the pieces are extremely simple and basic. The adjustment system is the same as the MGC Elite, with the enclosed spring and a stepped hand-adjustable spring compression with the screw just being a screw. 

 And realistically, all that the "speed micro-actuator" does is exist as a marketing strategy. I tried taking them out, and it made- wait for it- ZERO DIFFERENCE. I didn't feel a difference at all, so I'm tempted to take them out and put them into my MGC 4x4, where it apparently has a more noticeable effect. 

 anyway, I mentioned the YS3M. And it's very similar, only that it's cheaper and more fun. And I believe that it's fascinating that such a loved cube has now morphed into a cousin that's dissed for whatever random reason. I think that it's got serious potential. I really like it as a cube, and as a concept as a return to the golden age of hardware development. 

 And as a side note, hey Cubicle, you should visit the Speedsolving forums.

 As for cons I'm not sure if it's the way I have it tensioned, the cube being like this for many people, or if there really is something wrong with the specific Sigma I have, but the cube pops somewhat frequently. Due to this issue I have to dock a star from my review. review_title: Snappy and Addictive – The MGC Sigma Delivers
review_text:
What I love about the SIGMA is that satisfying, snappy sound. It is lightweight and turns much differently from the MGC Beta. I own both, and I find myself just doing random turns on the SIGMA because it sounds and feels so good. 

 The M moves are super smooth, which makes slice turns really addictive. It is one of those cubes you pick up just to do a few turns and end up playing with for a while. The cube feels very responsive and lively, which makes it fun to handle even when you are not actively solving. 

 Compared to the Beta, the SIGMA feels a bit sharper and more crisp in its turning. The Beta feels more muted, while the SIGMA gives you more feedback and that snappy sound that makes each turn satisfying. 

 I added two drops of Mystic just to stabilize it a little, and that made it even better to turn. It kept the cube fast but added just enough control to make the turning feel smoother. 

 Overall, this is a really fun cube to use, especially if you enjoy smooth M slices and a crisp, snappy turning feel.

It's a jing's pyraminx (corner turning) but with gears. It shapeshifts a lot and looks epic when scrambled. 

 It isn't that hard to solve. The worst you will encounter is an issue with one flipped edge, but that's not a true parity and is just something you just need to problem-solve around. But it's still harder than a gear cube, so get that first if you want to get into gear puzzles. 

 In addition to the corner turning moves, this puzzle also allows a satisfying edge turning move where you grip opposite edges and spin. Everything on the cube rotates simultaneously. You can even use this move to your advantage during the solve. 

 The main issue with the puzzle is that the mechanism can sometimes misalign and get stuck if you are too careless. This is mainly when you inadvertently perform the edge turning move when trying to turn the corners. When this happens, and you continue to perform moves, the whole puzzle can end up in an illegal position, requiring a slight disassembly to restore it. This is really annoying. 

 Despite this, I personally think it's a really cool puzzle. It's fun and pretty on the shelf and in the hand. I don't agree with the low average rating it got and would certainly recommend it to anyone who loves gear cubes.

Wow am I ever impressed with this! Straight out of the box it was basically ready to go. All I did was add a bit of lube to it. The ball bearings do give a click at the beginning and end of each turn, but the pieces have a "ramp-track" of sorts that make the transition so smooth that you'll never feel the bearings going over seams and said bearings do their job of keeping the layers aligned and providing feedback. Corner cutting is astonishing as you can basically cut an entire square-to-square area in the middle of a turn. Doesn't reverse much though, just as much as there is roundness on a piece. I got this in stickerless and they are the standard excellent QiYi shades with the exception of the blue which is of the lighter variety (Dunno why some have this while most others have a darker blue). No trouble telling shades apart even in low lighting. One thing I'm a little iffy on is the frosted surfaces. They feel more slippery than other stickerless cubes as a result of that finish. Other than that though, it's amazing!

review_title: A great next step for cubers!
review_text:
Difficulty: 1.5/10
 Playability: 8/10
 Quality: 10/10 

 OVERVIEW: The Dino Cube is the most basic version of a corner turning cubic puzzle. If you can solve a Pyraminx, the Dino Cube is no different; it's basically just Pyraminx corners. The whole cube can be solved intuitively, but the "sledgehammer" algorithm is useful to use, as well as a knowledge of the Rubik's color scheme for faster solving. For an added challenge, you can try to solve the Dino Cube in a checkerboard pattern, or with a set of opposite colors swapped. The turning on this cube is buttery smooth, and has a frosted finish. The plastic doesn't feel cheap, although some people may prefer a more glossy texture for a stickerless cube. 

 PROS: Smooth turning, fun to play with, and high quality build.
 CONS: The smoothness is sometimes too smooth, and with no alignment mechanism, you sometimes move other layer accidentally and re-align. You quickly get used to it, but it may slow down a solve slightly.

I got this in stickerless and you can tell the shades apart very nicely. I'd even say I prefer the light blue over the darker blue most others have as it looks more unique. One thing that Dino Cubes tend to have are lock ups though and that makes or breaks the fun factor in playing around with one. I'm pretty confident that Qiyi has managed to do the absolute best it could with this though because it flies from turn to turn. It is buttery smooth, corner cuts about 1/5 a piece (keep your expectations low here as it IS a dino and thus you can only ask for so much from the intersecting angles) and never seems to slow me down as lock ups are as non-existent as a Dino can probably be. The only thing I'm a bit iffy with is the frosted plastic. Sure it doesn't show scratches like glossy would, but it also doesn't have as much grip as glossy does. So you may want to give it a clear coat or polish the pieces to a shine.

The Thunderclap V3 M is a really nice budget cube for novices and professionals alike. It is a really nice speed cube if you are a starter as most speed cubes people start of with are on average worse than flagships, but beginners don't need flagships either. The best budget 3x3 OOTB today is most likely the RS3 M 2020, with some setup, the Qiyi MS, Thunderclap V3 M, and YuXin Little Magic M are all really nice; 
 The thunderclap v3 M is in essence a Valk 3 Power M but with cheaper plastic, but to me there's not much of a difference. The cube is a little tight, that is why it locks up a little on fast turns, loosening won't help as it will be too uncontrollable and snappy, so I recommend lubricating it with a heavy/gummy silicone lubricant like Angstrom Compound X, Max Command, or Traxxas 50k to make it more controllable. Under the springs I recommend Traxxas 50k as well. If lubricating with a heavy lube makes it slow, I recommend some Cubicle Silk or DNM-37 to speed it up. In conclusion this a nice cube, but OOTB it needs some setup, tensions are fine, it only needs lubricating, but after setup it is otherwordly. It is a Valk 3 Power M with cheaper plastic, but it has the potential of the Valk Power M.

review_title: Can figure it out intuitively, and make some nice designs
review_text:
Got this for Christmas along with a few other smaller non-WCA cubes. I didn't bother trying to speed-cube it because nobody cares about your redi-cube time, it's not a real event, most people have never even heard of it. 

 What I really enjoyed about it was the difficulty level -- it felt like a totally new puzzle, not just a 3x3 with a twist or something, but it was also manageable. I was able to figure out some invariants of how it moved and how to solve it, and put it together intuitively without having to go to google. And yet I also didn't solve it by accident or overly quickly; I had to take some time and figure it out. So I guess I'm reviewing redi cubes as a concept, not the MoYu redi cube specifically. 

 But this particular object is pretty good. The turning is fine, it doesn't catch too often, and I didn't have any trouble with it. I wouldn't try to speed-cube with it, the mechanisms would become frustrating, but again I didn't want to speed-cube with it, so I don't mind. 

 The stickerless facelets are fairly attractive, although it doesn't sit as perfectly as I might like, and so I enjoyed not only tinkering with it and trying to solve it, but making some nice designs with it. There are some interesting quirks of parity that make it a lot of fun to be creative with, I think. 

 Basically I could ding it a star if I wanted to because the motion isn't perfect, and the plastic isn't perfect, but I don't want to ding it a star, because I love this thing, and I carry it around and play with it, and my wife (not a cuber) plays with it, and my kids (3 and 6) play with it, and it's a hit, and I love it, and if you want one, you should buy one.
Overall love the cube, but magnets would make it easier to handle and I would have gladly paid extra for them.

review_title: Great, but way too much breaking in
review_text:
This cube started as a major disappointment out of the box: it was sandy, the finish was not grippy for me, and the stability was very poor. The magnetic system felt very unique- there was no distinct pulling between the layers; instead, it felt like tiny pegs fitting perfectly into holes in the pieces like you would find on a cheap pyraminx, holding the layers tight but lacking the tactile force expected in any magnetic cube, let alone a flagship.  

 However, after an extended break in period, this cube finally started to shine. It became much smoother, and it might just be me, but even the grip seemed to feel better. I didn't tension it, but I did lube it with some DNM-37 and a little FZ-Calm, which eliminated the slight gummy feeling it had and optimized the performance. The resulting speed is mid to slow, making it extremely comfortable, which is vital for a big cube.  

 While the cube can be stiff and locks up a fair amount, its durability is phenomenal; I have used this cube extensively and it has not once popped or even caught, making it very reliable. However, I did have a problem at one point in time where one of the red center caps would fall off during a solve, but once I stuck it back in probably a little too hard, I didn't have that problem again. This cube can sometimes be on the noisier side, but nothing that will affect your solves. The standard size makes it comfortable for just about anyone, and the weight is not bad for a 6x6. 

 This cube does have one major flaw though: the corner-cutting. For some reason, the piece design just doesn't allow for aggressive cuts, requiring precise turning even the MGC 6x6 doesn't need. 

 Despite the rough start and this single technical draw, its ultimate stability and control leads me to believe this is the best 6x6 on the market, excluding the new v4 models. It's a great cube for serious solvers, but due to the price and the time needed to break in, I would not recommend this cube for beginners. 4/5 stars. Good cube. review_title: Best 6x6 on the market by far
review_text:
Hey there! So, full disclosure, I'm not exactly a wordsmith, but I'm excited to share my thoughts on this product with you through a pros and cons list!
 Let's start with the positives:
 • This product offers an ideal combination of speed and control. It's fast, yet still provides a good level of control. Of course, the speed may vary depending on your setup.
 • The corner cutting ability of this puzzle is excellent. It can smoothly cut around 2 pieces, although this depends on the tensions that you use.
 • I hardly experience any popping issues with this cube, even though my turning style is a bit rough and imprecise. In my 20-30 solves, I have had maybe 2 or 3 pops, and most of those were when I first got this cube and had not gotten used to the turning. 
 • When compared to its competitors, this cube stands out as a superior option. The MGC suffers from excessive popping, while the Shadow V2 has subpar out-of-the-box performance and requires extensive setup to reach a satisfactory level.
 • Size-wise, this cube is pretty compact at 63mm. Additionally, it is very lightweight, weighing only 149 grams. For reference, the MGC 6x6 measures 65mm and weighs 175 grams. 

 Now, let's move on to the negatives (though most of them are minor nitpicks):
 • One drawback worth noting is the somewhat higher price of this puzzle, coming in at $44. The price is roughly on par with the Shadow V2 and $19 more expensive than the MGC.
 • Probably the most significant drawback is the fact that this cube has frosted plastic. It does not provide very good grip when compared to UV or glossy plastic. It's a puzzling design choice by MoYu. (Pun absolutely intended)
 • The magnets on this puzzle are relatively weak. For me, it was not as bad as I expected, but if you know that you like stronger magnets, then it might help to get a few RS3M+ magnet kits. Tip: You will need 4 magnet kits to add extra magnets to just the 2 inner layers, and one additional kit to doublestack the outer layer magnets. If you doublestack both of the magnets on the second layer, then you won't need to doublestack the magnets on the outer layer.

I got this cube for Christmas along with the Aochuang and Aofu WRM because my cubes were old; my old 5x5 popped at least 3 times each solve, my old 7x7 was way too big and my old 6x6 was broken ; Aoshi (this cube) was the best out of all. 6x6 hardware was notoriously bad, even though some cubes like Shadow or MGC were usable, they sometimes pop and catch . Aoshi WRM don't. It corner cuts better than some 5x5 (1.5 piece) ,even better than my new Aochuang WRM. 

 Unpopular Opinion: The only flaw of this 6x6 speedcube is the inner layers' magnets ; they were too strong. 

 Overall; after lubing it with Angstrom Dignitas and other lubes , this cube is probably the best 6x6 out there, I recommend it to people who have enough money to spend.
 Otherwise, you can get the MGC if your budget is under $45 but over $25 or the YJ Yushi M which is probably the cheapest 6x6 that's decent.

review_title: I'm no 6x6 expert but this thing is pretty good
review_text:
Hello. I'm a noob who has only had one other 6x6 in my life (what I think is this one's predecessor, the Aoshi GTS M, which is discontinued on TheCubicle) and this one far surpasses it. On the GTS M, the magnets are more even in strength between the layers, which means that sometimes when I turn the outer layer, the second innermost layer comes with it. On this one, I have no such problems. The outer layers are quick and smooth, and the inner layers have nice strong magnets that help keep them in place. Out of the box, it has that dry, sandy feeling that can easily be counteracted with lube. It's relatively smooth even without lubricant, though. I'm a big fan of MoYu cubes, especially their big cubes like the 4x4. The manufacturers have outdone themselves again! 

 A couple warnings:
 If you loosen the cube too much (which I wouldn't recommend doing for any big cube because it can pop) the screws sticking out a little bit from the centers causes them to bump against the pieces when you're turning, causing an unholy scraping/locking sensation. Tighten the screws until they sink in at least a little bit to prevent this. Since it's a fast cube anyway, you don't need it too loose.
 It may be a speedcube, designed for speed, but don't turn it too fast and abuse the corner cutting, because again, it will pop. This applies to any big cube, speedy or not.

review_title: MoYu Weipo WRS: Excellent cube at a reasonable price
review_text: I got this cube to replace my MGC Elite. I chose it because I could not find the Valk 2 for sale anywhere and didn't want to spend over $30 on a GAN 2x2. Out of the box, it was fast, a bit scratchy, and had that distinct "moyu feel" which I really liked.  After about 15 solves with no setup, I was already averaging what I normally did (3.6-3.7). I added weight 5, a little DNM, and increased the spring compression. After 100-150 solves the cube's performance exceeded my expectations. The most notable part was that the small corner cuts took virtually the same amount of effort as turning a fully aligned cube would. The cube felt smooth, quick, and airy. Overall, I much prefer this over the MGC Elite despite it being almost half the price and can recommend it to anyone looking for a high performing and customizable 2x2. I do believe my experiment will hopefully prove successful however, it has become significantly more controllable. I believe with the right setup this can still be salvaged into a very good pyraminx, but I still wouldn't place it high on my recommendation list. product_name: MoYu AoChuang V6 5x5 (Double-Track + Matte Special Edition)
review_text:
I got this version insetnad of the UV version as there are some concerns about Picube's UV being too thin. Also the matte on this cube is basically just glossy. 

 Ootb, this cube feels very fast and quite loose, and sometimes when I turned the outer layers, it would pick up the inner layers as well. Corner cutting is execellent and the size is very comfortable for me. The logo also has a very clean look. Setting up this cube was quite a pain due to the center caps having an anti-deforming mechanism. But once setup is done this cube becomes the best on the market. 

 For setup, I used PiLube Yellow (XMT 10 + FZ Calm is also really good) on the outer tracks and used Weight 5 on the inner tracks. I tightened the cube quite a bit and lubed the springs with more Weight 5. 

 After 20 solves, I can confidently say that the previous ootb issues are gone. It does come really close but I genuinely reccomend this over the GAN 562M after three days of solving.

review_text: I'm a slow cuber, and this review is superficial, so feel free to ignore it.  I think this is a really good 5x5 cube!  Out of the box, each layer turns easily and equally.  The outer layers turn like any good 3x3 cube.  Auto-alignment is good, the magnets are noticeable and effective but not annoyingly strong.  Corner cutting is good.  The cube doesn't seem to lock up and I've never had it pop.  The small size is convenient and not too small.  It's cheaper than the standard AoChuang V6 5x5 and better than the AoChuang V6 5x5 single-track, which is the only similar cube I can compare it too.  It's way better than the YJ MGC 5x5 cube.  I recommend it.

review_title: It doesn't get better than this, helped me go from sub 30 to sub 8.75, 6/5 star if possible.
review_text:
I've been using this cube for half a year now, and I can guarantee this is the best cube money can buy. 

 First of all, the price point is right. See those expensive Gan cubes? They are overpriced. I have pretty much all the flagship Gan cubes(12 mag uvc, 11 pro uvc) and I can safely say that this cube reigns them all. This is because that this cube is stable and quick, but not the best. Because this cube is a lot less than the Gans', you can use it as your main and will not have to worry TOO much if it gets destroyed. 

  As the cube itself, you probably will want to buy some kind of upgrade kit such as the CH Moyu RS3M core magnet upgrade kit. That is the one I applied to make it so much better. Without it, the magnet strength is a bit weak and it will feel a bit uncontrollable. So I STRONGLY recommend buying the corner-core upgrade kit to enhance this cube's performance. You will not regret it.  

 With the right setup, this cube delivers the perfect combination of speed and stability, which allows you to get some crazy fast times. OOTB, it is a bit sandy and clicky, but with time and using it it will wear away.  

 Next, I guarantee you it will not break. I have dropped this cube way too many times, and the cube just does not want to shatter. Even when it does, its usually easily fixable. 

 Lastly, I can prove that this cube is amazing. When it is the main of someone who averages mid-8's on 3x3 (no cap), you can make your own decision. This cube has always been my main since April of 2022, when I started cubing. I have tried many other cubes from many other brands, but at the end of the day, this will still be my main.

review_title: A Great Cube and a cool Innovation
review_text: I picked up this cube because I think it was on sale when I got it, my newest 3x3 was 4 years old, no magnets, and I also wanted to see how Maglev feels (And how magnets in general feel, haha). I like the super affordable price point. When I first got the cube it was really sandy so I didn't know what to expect, but I figured I should break it in a bit and see how it feels. And... Oh my goodness this cube is awesome. So essentially Maglev is different from regular springs in that it replaces them with two repelling magnets, and you can set the force between them with a little plastic adjuster that comes with the cube. After a couple days, I can confidently say that this cube is my new main. One reason is that it turns like butter, but is still fast, and the magnets help to keep the cube in shape while I turn it like a madman. The second reason this cube is my new main is because I got a new PB using this cube the night I unboxed it.

Good light cube and very fast, my only problem was that I found it a bit too fast for my turning style which resulted in lockup’s. However take this stance with a gran of salt as this is my opinion before fine tuning the cube (wich I’ve never been good at.

First of all, I got the Celeritas lube service (which I recommend) and because this cube is so fast out of the box, the lube really helps it become more controllable. This cube is great for beginner - intermediate level cubers, or if you are a very advanced cuber, this also works. Straight out of the box, it was smooth, no spring ping, and it turned amazing. I recommend this cube 100% to anyone who wants a better pb ;D
