review_title: A great cube that feels somewhere between the GAN 12 and 356 M to me
review_text:
I love this cube. I didn't think I would, which makes it weird that I bought it, in hindsight. I already had the frosted version of the 356 MagLev and wasn't entirely satisfied with it. I'm a casual solver and fidgeter, and the 356 M is my favorite GAN cube. It has a soft flexibility that I really like a lot. I also have the GAN 12, but I find that too unforgiving, like going off-road without shocks. 

 I've discovered I prefer UV coating, so for some reason I decided to try the 356 MagLev again, this time with UV. Out of the box I was amazed at how great it felt. I realize now that I had over-tightened and over-lubed the frosted one, and I prefer the stock settings, or close to them. 

 My favorite GAN is stlll the 356 M, but the 356 MagLev is a close second, and its feel to me is somewhere between the 356 M and the 12. It has some of the soft flexibility of the M and some of the crunchier feel of the 12. I think this could be a good middle ground for people who find the 12 as unforgiving as I do but maybe find the 356 M too far from that feel for their tastes.

review_title: I always come back to the 356 Maglev
review_text:
I wanted to like all of the rest. I tried the WRMV10, but the colors and UV don't pop like GAN. Tried Tornado V3, but the magnets and the noise didn't feel solid like GAN. Tried GAN14, and it feels pretty good but still come back to the 356 Maglev every time. I don't know what it is, but something about the speed, light weight, not needing to fiddle with corner magnets, all combined with the GAN quality coating, colors and manufacturing. It just feels quality and feels good in your hands every time! 

 As others have mentioned, this one will tend to lock up on occasion. The maglev adjustments on this one also favor a much looser center travel than most, so it is a little difficult to find the sweet spot.  

 Overall, I think this is a real fast and flowy cube that will appeal to those who prefer a loose grip, a light touch, and a casual-fast cubing style.

Before I start, I should mention that the only GAN 3x3 I’ve owned and tested is the 356 M. The 356 M has some issues with lockups, corner twists, and just being generally too uncontrollable. I’ve heard some similar complaints about other GAN 3x3’s with lockups being a major point. I’ve also heard that the GAN 12 is regarded as one of their best releases—outperforming the 13, 14, and maybe even 15. I personally have only ever tried the 356 M and the NewBlack but I have to say, the NewBlack is an outstanding cube.  

 I usually main the WRM 10 with other cubes interspersed here and there, but I think the NewBlack might be one of my favorite cubes I’ve used so far. Compared to the previous complaints of GAN cubes, I have only ever experienced minor lockups here and there which is likely a setup or user error. It’s smooth, controllable, and overall less prone to lockups out of the box. I love the GAN color-way and the black internals really make this cube POP. Overall, I enjoy the simple adjustment system, overall feel, and unique experience. 

 The only reason the cube doesn’t get 5 stars is because of its steep price point. MoYu is able to keep their Weilong series relatively cheap with remarkable cubes that compete with GAN’s line of 3x3’s and even their NewBlack.

review_title: Swift Block 355S Wow... amazing for the price
review_text:
So originally I was very doubtful of this cube. For $12 you couldn't possibly get a good cube. Or can you? So I ordered this cube and I tried it. I was amazed. I have tried lots of GAN cubes before. Even magnet ones. This cube struck out to me. The cube has a frosted finish which, well can be scratched rather easily if you're looking forward to removing the center caps. The cube in the factory settings is just right for me, which can depend on what type of cuber you are. Then comes the magnets. The name Swift Block is a pretty accurate name for the cube. The magnets are blocky, but good to the point where it gives you a satisfactory feeling when you cube, and the magnets are slightly weaker than GAN'S 356 M. If you don't prefer magnets, this might be a good option for you to try out magnet cubes. This cube is very Swift, hence the name. The cube with a bit of pressure in factory settings can turn 360 degrees, but usually with finger-flicks you can do about 180. Not everything is good though. The only complaint I have is that it pops if you have tweaked with your screws or the dial (i'll get to that). This cube has a decent range of customization. First, you can turn a dial which is located in the center piece. The dial won't do much, but well it's kinda cool. The second and the last one is that the screws can loosen to a nice feeling without bursting too easily, as the magnets kinda force it to stay together.
 Overall, this cube is definitely worth the money and is a 5-star product. The good outweighs the bad massively, so trying this friendly budget cube can save a lot of pocket money.

The magnets give the cube a satisfactory feel while cubing and you don't have that hand/arm fatigue feeling after solving a clunky Rubik's cube for $5 .This is amazing. You should buy this NOW!

When I purchased this, I wasn't expecting much honestly. It blew me away though. 

 Appearance: This cube has frosted plastic which usually means a slippery cube but I have had no trouble gripping this cube in fact it feels just the same as others for grip. The shades look nice. In the picture the green looks more lime green but in reality it's more of a natural green. Also the red isn't quite as bright as in the picture, but they look nice.  

 Feeling: This cube has a very odd feel. It feels sandy, papery, and really light, almost fragile feeling. It is definitely odd at first but you get used to it. It turns smoothly despite the sandy feeling and it's quite pleasant to use. 

 Performance: Out of the box this isn't that great. After a few solves however it feels pretty good. The flexibility and corner cutting are very impressive. Outer layer it does 1 and 3/4 of a piece, and inner does 3/4 of a piece. Reverse is about 1 piece for outer layer and 1/2 of a piece for inner layer. The only 4x4 I can compare this too is my Mofang Jiaoshi MF4 because it's all I own, but I must say for a cube that's half the price, it is better than the MF4 surprisingly. The factory tensions in my opinion are far too loose, which leads me to the issue this cube has: It catches sometimes. I have not had it pop yet and I've done some crazyyy overshooting, so popping is not an issue. If you've ever used an Mf5 5x5, then you know that the outer layers catch sometimes. This cube feels the same. It is fast but when you are sloppy it catches easy which may be frustrating for advanced solvers with high tps. I lubed my cube with a lot of Qiyi oil based lube and now it's smooth. It originally comes dry with no lube which isn't much fun to solve with, this is a cube you really need to lube. The outer layers are fun and you can do most CFOP algs on it quite easily yes even H and Z perms. If you have a light turning style this isn't the best cube for you because it does feel disappointing after using something like a gan air 3x3, for example, finger tricking the D layer during an E perm is hard on here. The inner layers feel a little sluggish but the lube helps and it's not too bad, just not amazing either. Outer layers are definitely better. One thing that I like that the MF4 can't do is the corner cutting. The inner layers on this may be slow but the 3x3 stage is quite fun. The catching does bother me but for the price you can't ask for better, this cube is amazing.  

 Conclusion:
 I believe this is a great cube for beginners and intermediates. Even a good backup for precise advanced solvers. Also fun for casual solving. 

 Overall for the price you can't go wrong. It's a great cube to have in your collection and the best cube you can buy for this low of a price.

review_text:
I ask myself what's the Big deal with the Big Cubes?; and the simple answer is... they are awesome! In Comparing the YuXin Super Big 3x3 (8.8cm) cube, to the HeShu Super Big 3x3 (18cm) cube, the DianSheng Super Big 3x3 (13cm) cube and the Guomeng Crazy Foot 10cm Cube. The Yuxin in my opinion, is much better than the Heshu Super Big cube in many aspects; when dealing with corner cutting, movability and solving enjoyment, it tops the Heshu in every way. Though the Heshu has amazing structural plastic; and it is Big! One cubie is the same size as a standard Rubik's Cube! Though the main problem with the Heshu, are the seals under the cubies; the seal that joins the individual two pieced cubie together. They catch pretty bad, making a 90 degree turn impossible at times; leaving your only option a 270 degree rotation. The Yuxin definitely surpasses, by leaps and bounds, the Guomeng Crazy Foot cube. It is in fact better in each and every way possible; corner cutting, plastic quality, sticker quality, movability and overall workmanship. Lastly to The DianSheng... It is an Amazing cube and I rate the Yuxin and the DianSheng exactly even. They are totally different in feel and structure; but the movability, durability, collectability and playability are totally awesome in both cubes. The only flaw I had with the Yuxin out of the box, was that it had excess hardened glue, or plastic (it's hard to tell because of the cubes transparency). Though a little cleanup mod, using a file and a damp cloth; it's now a 4 Star Cube. In closing; if you enjoy solving and collecting Big Cubes, then this is a good one to have.
  #oOpS I totally forgot that the Yuxin had tiles? In my previous review of the Yuxin Super Big Cube, I thought it had stickers! I am used to the LanLan 4x4 extruding tile structure and I totally overlooked The Smooth Tiles on the Yuxin Super Big: #oOPs. Well, they are good quality tiles and the color scheme is bright, vibrant and very "tiley". I can't see me wearing these tiles out anytime soon. review_text: This cube is a great addition to the Yuxin family. It is a very fast turning cube, but if that is not your thing, you can always slow it down with some heavier lube. It has a great floating feeling during turns, making it very fluid. Shades are on the better side for stickerless cubes, and the logo that comes on it is easily removable if you want to place your own there. The magnets can definitely be felt, and is one of the better mass-produced magnetic cubes. I was not a huge fan of the Yuxin Little Magic's stickerless version due to the frosted plastic, but this cube has the standard smooth feeling plastic which I am happy with.

Let me start off by saying that this cube is an absolute main killer! My old cube was a Little Magic M from CH, and it barely stands in comparison to this. OOTB, the cube is buttery-smooth and quite fast. I broke the cube in after about 150 solves. After that, I set the cube up with Weight 5 in the core and Weight 2 and DNM on the pieces. After quite a bit of lubey fingers and breaking in, this is one of the best cubes I've ever felt. Quite a bit slower than before, but still totally within my speed range. The magnets in the cube are pretty strong and noticeable while turn, but they don't interfere with speed much. The ball bearing weights in the corners do affect turning momentum, and I decided to keep them in for the purpose of keeping the speed in check when I put the lube in the cube. 

 Besides the cube, the box was very nice, and it came with a manual on how to solve a cube with ALL of the OLL and PLL algs on it as well as notation, of course. In the box was the cube and a bag for replacement washers, magnets, and ball bearings, which did come in handy after I accidentally dropped a ball bearing on my thick carpet.

review_title: Great feel - light and fast with satisfying feedback
review_text:
This cube is my main. I love the smooth, fast feeling and the satisfying tactile and auditory feedback with each turn. It's not too loud or too clicky, it's just right. The magnets feel prefect to me as well. 

 When I first got it, I didn't like the dry feeling so I overlubed it with Traxxas 30k. This made me dislike the cube for a while, but now that I came to my senses and wiped out most of the lube, it feels amazing. If you want to lube it, just the tiniest bit of silicone on the corner and edge stems should do the trick. 

 The two cubes that feel the best to me are the Huanglong and the MF3RS3M. They are somewhat similar, but now that I've set up the Huanglong properly, it has surpassed the RS3M. The Huanglong is quite a bit lighter, and the good qualities are magnified. I also prefer the shades on the Huanglong, for both the stickered and stickerless versions - in fact, these are my favorite stickerless shades (I like the darker green). 

 As for the ball bearing corner weights, I took them out, then put them back in, then forgot about them.

When i recieved it, the magnets was a little loose, and after a couple of months, 4 of the cornermagnets and 3 of the edge magnets had fallen out, so i glued every magnet in place myself to make sure they dont fall out anymore. But the turning quality is pretty good, Buttery smooth and really fast.

I think this is a great cube, and it is my new main over an MGC and YLM. It is very smooth and has an airy. When I got it ootb, it was actually really slow and wouldn't corner cut well, so I was disappointed. However, I loosened the tensions and started corner cutting at first small amounts, and then slowly increasing by about 5 degrees every now and then. After that, it was great at corner cutting, and the speed was perfect. 
 Then I lubed it with weight 5 on the core, and put a bit of weight 3 on the base of a corner stalk, with 3 drops of Martian to finish it off. Then it was godly, with a buttery smooth and extremely light feeling. It was able to get me a 17 sec pb solve. It was amazing.
  I must say that the magnets are much weaker than I expected, and I can't feel them in algs. They do their job though, and I just wish they were stronger, but it flows extremely well right now, and I expect too strong of a magnet may have prevented a well flowing cube.
 Overall, this is a great cube and I would definitely recommend it.
 By they way, to me the ball bearings didn't really make a difference whether they were in or out

These bright YuXin puzzles always turn very nicely, and have a great feel overall {I have yet to need to adjust any tensions, nor lube their puzzles... maybe after a few years of enjoyment...?  Nice to have the ability if ever needed!}.  This puzzle offers notably more challenge than many of their other larger and unusual shaped puzzles. 

 I got this as a 'shape mod' of the XJ Curvy Face-Turning Rhombic Triacontahedron (Plus), as this edge-turning version's colouring doesn't have specificity of placement of the trifoliums' parts.  I really enjoy having the option of doing a standard mixup as well as a jumbling mixup, so I encourage getting the Ultimate so one has that option for a future challenge! 

 The ease of movement means you can quickly walk pieces around the puzzle to the place you want them without any delays from fighting the puzzle's finickiness.  The size is quite manageable (identical to mf8's icosahedron puzzles), and is delightfully lightweight.  The colours are all vibrant and distinct, but if you are using a warm and/or dim bulb at night, a couple of the colours can look rather similar with that yellow ambient light (pro tip: keep an LED flashlight on hand to verify the colours do actually match). 

 I was very happy to add this variant to the collection, and the challenge level is just right!

review_text:
TLDR: out of the box it is not great but after a couple solves it breaks in nicely and is a fantastic cube. 

 Long review: When I first got the puzzle I was pretty disappointed. Specifically turning between layers 4-5 and 7-8 was absolutely horrible, and this was the case for all sides. I got this because I don’t have an icosahedral puzzle. Without much thought, I took a look, thought it would be a big Redi Cube, and figured it would be easy but manageable, do a couple quick solves, put it on a shelf, and wait for a proper FTI to come out. 

 Not so. It’s a curvy copter. Now I did own one, but I never learned how to solve it properly, as the jumbling frightens me. So I scrambled this in the same way, careful not to jumble it, and solved it a few times. The motion is pretty good! Not incredible, it’s not a speed cube, but I haven’t had lockups or pops or anything. It’s high quality. 

 So that was fine. But then my son accidentally jumbled it, then misremembered how to undo it, and long story short I’m working through it myself. I finally learned how to solve the original copter— by necessity, hoping the ideas would help out here, which they sort of do — and now I’m still partway through my first jumbled solve here. Loving it. 

 As for the two editions, it’s your choice which you think is harder. The regular is like a traditional copter, which means it bandages. The ultimate has an extra slit, which means all those bandaged turns actually can be moved, which means your pieces can split up further. 

 I got the ultimate by accident; but upon reflection I think it might actually be easier, although I’m not sure. I haven’t had much trouble pairing the edges back together (although it could make your solve very very long if you split them all). Either way, I suspect both versions are an excellent choice.

product_name: MFJS Mirror Cube 3x3 V2 (Magnetic + Ball-Core + UV)
review_title: The Best Mirror Cube on the Market
review_text:
I have a collection of nearly every magnetized mirror cubes available since the GAN Mirror when it released. I nodded my GANs by sanding down the sharp corners which were designed to prevent corner twists, and added some magnets in the corner pieces to increase the stability. It was (and still is) a great puzzle. 

 I recently got the gold Moyu Mirror v2 with the ball-core, and I have to say it’s the best I’ve tried. As the former Canadian unofficial mirror cube NR holder for single and average, I can say I prefer this. I’ve also modded this to make the magnetic feel even stronger, using the RS3M magnet kit and adding 2 magnets per edge piece, allowing looser tensions without loss in stability. Easily my favourite mirror cube now, and aesthetically pleasing. 

 Critiques: limited loosening potential from the small side like many say. Can cut the spring to loosen further, but I can handle it as it currently is. Also, the plastic in places can be quite thin. Other than that, I find this to be the perfect puzzle for me. I highly recommend increasing the magnetic strength for faster solving with higher stability.

review_text: The turning is very smooth, and, for a mirror blocks cube, the corner cutting is great. The magnets are on the stronger side, but they're not too strong. They make the cube nice and stable. I love that there's a silver option unlike the GAN. The shortest layer is difficult to tension without making the center cap bulge too much, but I was able to find a good enough screw depth. Given the design of the mirror blocks cube in general, I'm not sure how avoidable this issue is.

review_title: It had a good run, good cube though.
review_text:
Let's start off from the beginning. When I unboxed it, it was really quite good. It turned fairly well, the packaging was well done, and overall it was a good first impression. It didn't corner cut though, but honestly, who goes and buys an 11x11 expecting the corner cutting to be good, so that's not what the lost star is for. 

 But now let's get into why I put 4 stars instead of 5. This is because this is not the best cube out there, particularly not the best 11x11 out there, and this is to be expected, because it's clearly not meant to be. When solving this cube you can't go super fast, or else it will lock up really bad. This cube is not a speedcube, so if you are trying to speedcube with an 11x11, this cube isn't for you. But, for casual solving it's amazing, it's nice and small so your hands fit nicely around it, it turns really quite good when you're not turning at the speed of light, and in general it's just nice to sit back and solve this cube. 

 But now for the main reason a lot of people will probably be buying this cube. At $92, it's got to be one of, if not the cheapest 11x11 out there. And for the price, this cube preforms outstandingly. No your turns per second is not going to be through the roof, but for $92, you are definitely getting what you pay for in an 11x11, and a little more. 

 A lot of the people giving this cube bad reviews are saying that the turning is really bad and that it exploded when they first got it. If this is the case, then they just weren't careful with their cube, but if you're careful with this cube then you should be fine. Take me for an example, this is an example of what not to do when you get your 11x11. I was walking up to my front door, and tried to open the door with my 11x11 in the same hand, big mistake. I ended up accidentally dropping the cube, and the cube shattered on my front porch. I don't know what I'm doing to do about my 11x11, but I'll figure it out, but I'm not taking stars off because that was my fault. I also did this with my MF9 a while back. 

 So if you're going to take anything from that story, please just be careful with it, especially when bringing it out in public, because this cube isn't meant to stand getting dropped, and let me tell you, don't test it, unless of course that's the reason you're buying this cube. 

 TL;DR (too long, didn't read), this cube is not for speedcubing by any means, and it will lock up and perhaps shatter if you try speedcubing with it, but if you're not looking to speedcube with it, and you're just looking for a good budget 11x11, this cube is for you. Coming at $92 you are definitely getting what you pay for, and perhaps a little more. If you do buy it, though, you have to be careful with it, never risk bringing it anywhere, try not to speedcube with it, and most importantly never drop it. Learn from a guy who dropped his 11x11 and it shattered. 

 Overall great cube, would recommend to anyone looking for an amazing budget 11x11.

 The Standard Dode is smooth, well-built, no popping, and brilliantly stickered.  It is the right size not to cramp your hands during long solves.  The algs are rhythmic and some are easy to remember.  Getting out of the jumbled state is scary!!
 Overall, strategy and set-ups can get extremely tricky and frustrating.  But in the end, you find a way resolve.  Placing the 4-color corners was the most challenging for me as this is where you discover the reversed center which shows up as an apparent parity of the 4-color corners.  Undoing the reversed center is not too bad but certainly breaks your stride toward the next stage.  
 My favorite stage is placing the triangles, as it is fun and involves strategic set-ups to keep track of!.  
 The final stage of placing the three-color triangles is exciting and easy but one could easily get tripped up toward home base if you're tired.  
 I definitely recommend the Standard Doderhombus.  This is the right mix of mind-bending, scary challenge and plain fun jumbling.  You will not be bored. Can't wait to solve again!!!

review_title: A dry puzzle with a ton of potential
review_text:
This Moyu kilominx is something quite special if you are willing to put in the time and effort. Upon disassembling the puzzle, I found that every single piece was completely bone dry. Why MoFang JiaoShi (Moyu) decided to do this, I'll never know.  My next complaint comes from the screw types.  The heads of these screws are slightly larger than a normal moyu puzzle.  If you use one of the Moyu screw drivers to try to loosen them then you might end up stripping the screws (They also happen to be very tight and hard to move).  Luckily, I had a proper screw driver and I was able to get this thing apart without much problem.  And from there is actually where the final complaint comes in for this puzzle; its tensions are all very tight out of the box which leads to numerous catches. All of these issues can be overcome with a little elbow grease.  I took the time to loosen all of the screws a few turns and I made sure that they were all about the same upon inspection.  I also added some Weight 5 to the screws and the springs to make sure that the core was properly lubed.  I then was able to reassemble the puzzle and add a bit of mystic, silk and DMN lube on a couple of the pieces.    

 After break in I was pretty impressed.  This Kilominx is as good as it can be without magnets, that is to say that it will still catch a little bit if the layers are misaligned but other then that small complaint, the puzzle turns as good as any mid tier megaminx.  If you have this puzzle or are looking for a good kilominx and are not afraid to get your hands a little dirty, then I highly recommend you take a shot at setting one up for yourself. I do hope one day that Moyu decides to make a magnetic variant and until then I may just try to add magnets to this thing myself.

review_title: Challenging puzzle with dubious colors and needs to house-broken
review_text:
I got the non-stickered / colored-plastic version because it was the only available.  I'm disappointed my preference isn't available, but I don't blame The Cubicle . com because I searched the web for sticker version without success.  I'm trying to review without that factor in mind... 

 This is 4x4 version of face-turning octohedron (FTO).  In my opinion it should be a *little* bigger than classic 3x3 FTO, but the two are virtually identical in size.  In other words, each block of this puzzle is pretty small.  Like the 3x3 version, it is slightly bigger than classic 3x3 Rubik's Cube.  I think it should be a little bigger... 

 It is stiff to turn out-of-the box despite being well-lubricated.  In fact the entire puzzle felt oily/greasy out-of-the-box... this feeling wore off quickly after about 30 minutes of play.  Despite the lubrication, it is stiff to turn brand-new.  In fact, I thought you could only turn the outer-most face/layer when I began playing with it.  But in fact, you can turn two layers deep (effectively turning 1/2 the polyhedron).  Out-of-the-box a 2-layer-deep turn is EXTREMELY stiff.  

 The colored plastic quality seems pretty good (this is the first serious non-stickered puzzle I've bought), but I **HATE** the color scheme.  I can understand it might be a bit different than other stickered octohedrons, but I own several and the colors are inconsistent with EVERYTHING else.  I could even forgive the non-standard scheme if it worked well, but pink and light-orange are hard to distinguish (even though they are adjacent colors!) 

 However, after playing with it for a few hours, the turning was more reasonable.  It even allows a mild bit of corner-cutting, but is not for speed-cubing.  If you are slow and methodical, it will still occasionally jam.  Not a big surprise considering all the many sharp-cornered pieces!  It took me a few days to solve it, and it only once popped a piece.  If you get in a hurry, expect it to jam a lot and occasionally pop pieces. 

 I guess this all sounds negative, and it *IS* a bit pricey.  But despite the color issues and stiffness out-of-the-box, I give it 4 stars because it is a challenging puzzle; the only 4x4 FTO that I've seen recently; and it really plays smoother once broken-in.  The non-standard colors don't lend well to a collection, unless you like bizarre.

review_text: I had previously purchased the Void Pentultimate and discovered it was almost unusable, it caught and locked up constantly, the centers caps would just fall out, and occasionally the rail system would just break and start to come apart. This is a deep cut corner turning icosahedron. It looks simple and cool but its solve is very tedious, practically requiring you to swap and cycle pieces until solved. This is made worse by the fact that it is so large and is very catchy, causing hand cramps. And there is a really annoying parity you have to deal with. As a result, it really isn't that much fun to play with. Sticker quality is decent though, and the box is pretty cool. If you want a much better icosahedron puzzle for your collection, check out the AJ Clover Icosahedron. That is much more fun, turns better, and is prettier.

First, the good:
   The puzzle is wonderful, and I’m very glad to have finally gotten one!  It turns wonderfully once you stop pulling the pieces in the other hemisphere away with your grip (better to gently push all towards the equator instead).  The puzzle is essentially a 6-axis skewb with pentagonal faces having orientation, and triangular corners which do not.  Also, if you have never handled or seen an icosahedral mf8 puzzle in person, this is huge!  It measures in at 100mm face-to-face, but only 364g, so there is no problem getting a good grip on the puzzle itself.  Like all mf8 large form puzzles, this is not a speed cube, it is just a long-solve puzzle that moves well. 

 Now, the weird:
   The first and most annoying thing was how I could see through the bag and case that it was already stickered.  Opening the ziplock bag showed the sealing sticker of the case had been opened on three sides, leaving the back as a makeshift hinge.  Many of the stickers are offset well beyond my tolerances, just emphasizing how much I wanted to do it myself.  The colour sequence itself seems fairly random too, neither following the common twizzle.net layout, nor any other mass produced icosahedral puzzle I could locate.  Heck, I would have preferred to mimic Meffert’s 10 colour Dogic’s rainbow layout over this.  I will say, the stickers are extremely well stuck on, and I think I would not end well if I tried to carefully peel them to realign, let alone reorder, so I will stick with this ad hoc choice.  Side note: I’m surprised mf8 included two orange sides that look so much alike!  Another reason to use a rainbow carousel colour scheme for this puzzle! 

 So, I know this puzzle is very hard to locate, but I rather wish I had had a heads up that this was an open box and I would not have a choice in the stickering.  It didn’t appear to be lubed or broken in, so the person clearly just opened it, stickered it, played with it for a bit, then decided it would be a shelf piece and passed it on… but mostly I had no idea that The Cubicle would pass on previously owned items to customers, especially without telling us.  I am glad to have finally got one of these, but I’m sad to not have had the full unboxing and stickering experience with the purchase. 🙋🏼‍♀️

I don't often review things, but this blew me away, so i had to.  I came into buying this very excited because it thought it was just a cheep stickerless clover cube.  I thought i was getting a god deal, little did i know it was not a clover cube at all.  Probably should have read the description... lol.  Anyways, when i got it i was very confused about how it  turned, until i realized it is just a 3x3 shape mod with no centers (unless you spreed out the pieces and look inside).  I went back here and saw it was a 3x3 shape mod and not a clover cube and i was disappointed, but not for long.  I scrambled it and almost completed it with just two corners flipped, but i couldn't figure out how to do it, so i took it apart.  I put it back together smiling.  I had just found my new favorite puzzle.  Out of the 200+ puzzles in my collection, this was my favorite.  I played with it some more and here is a list of pros and cons of the cube: 

 Pros:
 1.  Patterns (checkerboard, etc.) looks really cool
 2. Simple, yet hard to solve
 3. strange parities.
 4. Nice out of the box turning
 5. Good price
 6. Neat puzzle disguised as a clover cube 

 Cons:
 1. If you have a bad turning style, it can hurt to turn
 2. If your to lazy to figure out parity. it can't be solved
 3. could trick people (Like me) into thinking its a clover cube 

 Over all, its an amazing puzzle.  None of the cons can really be fixed due to the nature of the puzzle. My one suggestion is for it to be called by a different name so it could be more easily recognised.  Other then that great puzzle!  Thanks Cubicle!

review_text:
This pyraminx is usable but not good. At this price range, the puzzle it has to beat is the QiYi MS pyraminx, and it doesn't come close. The corner cutting is poor, and the tips aren't magnetic at all. The tips are very stiff and tend to get stuck halfway through a turn if you just flick them. This puzzle also comes bone dry with no lube whatsoever and feels very scratchy ootb, however a bit of XMT-10 (or silk, martian, etc; any light silicone lube will work) vastly improves the feel of turning and smooths things out. 

 Given all that, just buy the QiYi MS. The MS pyra, costing only $1 more, has magnetic tips, better corner cutting, and comes lubed out of the box.

review_text: Out of the box, this puzzle is incredibly slow and stiff. I was able to make it usable by loosening it, adding lubricant, and partially sanding down the bumps on the centers. However, even after all of this work, it is not as good as the similarly-priced QiYi MS and YuXin Little Magic M which are usable out of the box.

 A 5-second web search for “Map of the world cube projection” could’ve solved this, but instead we got this careless shortcut.

review_title: Little Magic clone with some minor differences.
review_text:
If you want a YLM, but don't want to spend an extra dollar, this is basically it.  

 The feeling is almost identical, which is harsh and clicky with good flexibility, but it admittedly feels slightly denser than the YLM, though I had to have them side by side and closely pay attention to it. It also was slightly less compact as well. 

 Mechanically, the YBK is around 80% identical to the YLM. They both feature a three step center and edge design, sloped center caps, and similar track patterns on the corners.  

 However, the YBK doesn't have separate bases for the stickerless splits, such that Corners are three piece and edges are two piece. The YBK also has a slightly shallower design than the YLM, which is why it feels less compact. Since the corners are split at the base, the YBK isn't as hollow sounding as the YLM, though still rather loud. The finish on the YBK is also different. While the YLM is more of a frosted, grainy feel, the YBK is more matte than it is frosted, which I Personally really enjoy because it gives a slightly better grip, though it may pose a problem for dropping your cube in a material like dirt, because it may be difficult to remove the stains.  

 In conclusion: This cube is a bargain if you want a stickerless little magic. I would also like to add that the YBK comes much better straight out of the box than the YLM. This cube is definitely a steal.

This is okay, but not nearly as good as higher end puzzles. Out of the box, the body was quite nice. It had a quick, smooth feel with a light click after each turn from the ball bearings, which are interestingly in the edges rather than the centers. However, the tips were so clicky that they were essentially unusable. Normally, this wouldn't be a problem, as the springs for the ball bearings could be switched for softer ones. However, in order to reduce production costs, YuXin used a different design that makes this impossible. Rather than the traditional ball bearing and spring design, this puzzle has protrusions on the tips that fit into grooves on the centers, making them nonadjustable without modding, which is what I ended up doing. I sanded down the protrusions, which helped drastically. After the modification and setup, this puzzle is average. It maintains the original feel, which is a positive for me, but the relatively poor cornercutting causes some minor lockups and catches, making solves less fluid. Additionally, the stickers are fairly poor quality. I put a significant gouge in one of the yellow stickers just from removing the logo. My times on this puzzle are about half a second slower on this puzzle compared to my main X-Man Bell, which is significant as a sub-4.5 second solver. Overall, I would really only recommend this puzzle to people who are on a budget and are willing to do the mod, but I think most people should pass on this one.

review_text: This is a classic cube and it was my first "real" cube coming from a Rubik's brand puzzle. It's crazy how cheap, reliable, and versatile this cube is. Everything about it is the model of what a beginner/casual cube should be, but it's also got something special about it. It's incredibly light and won't tire your hands after long solving sessions. It's very stable, even without magnets, and it wants to keep it's cube shape, even if you set it up loose. Tighten it down and it doesn't feel 'squeezed' or 'pinched'. It's great when set up to your preferences and it's even good right out of the box; well-tensioned with a little lube. This a great, cheap cube to take to the beach, the park, camping or anywhere you don't want to take your fancy cubes. Perfect for kids and beginners, Everyone should have at least one around. review_text:
ootb it was way too tight and was bone dry. After messing around with tensions and adding lube, it is amazing. Corner cutting and speed was perfect. It has a fast and crunchy feel.  Overall after the setup, it's definitely a contender with some of the best 4x4's out there. review_title: Great as a new challenge, flawed in quality
review_text:
So, I bought this puzzle to try new things to solve, and my gosh is this one of the hardest things I've tried. The second after I finished scrambling, I was already lost as I didn't even know which piece was what so it seemed like I had no starting place. But over time, I found properties of the puzzle and strategies that helped me work toward the solution, which I'll let the user find out for themselves. 

 That said, there is one flaw in the quality of this puzzle. One I would like to address is it doesn't turn the best. It isn't utterly terrible either as there's not much friction between the pieces, but it also barely corner cuts. But this, I find acceptable as it's not meant to be a speed cube. What I find to be more of a bother, though, is the lenticular colors. Some of these colors don't mask the other colors well, especially the light ones. From some angles, it feels like the colors are blended together (I'm aware of our double vision, but it holds even if I have one eye closed) and it makes it even harder to tell what each color's supposed to be. This really brings down the solving experience a bit, especially when it's already tough (yeah, it's supposed to be tough, but from the confusion on which of the two colors to use, not from the incomplete masking of darker colors). 

 Overall, I had fun with this puzzle, both in its challenge and in its aesthetics. But it had needless sources of frustration at times.

The Skewby Copter plus is an amazing feat of design.  By combining a curvy copter plus with a skewb, it adds multiple levels of additional complexity and creates a new, unique puzzle challenge.   For example, doing a half skewb move unlocks a completly new turning option not available on any other curvy copter.  And that's just one of many new features the skewb turning introduces.  But even if the skewb features are a bit too daunting for you, it is still worth purchasing as it is quite simply the best designed curvy copter on the market.  This puzzle is designed so it is virtually impossible to bandage.   When jumbled, pieces that would collide on a normal curvy copter slide right by each other.   The only issue I have had with this puzzle are some of the small edge pieces falling out when doing jumbling moves.  Really it was just one edge piece that kept falling out.  Gluing the sides of these edge pieces together solves that problem.  But everything else has been great.  The turning is really smooth and the stickers are high quality.  I recommend this puzzle to anyone who likes a challenge.

review_title: Excellent puzzle with an excellent design
review_text: The Skewby Copter Plus is an excellent puzzle that even improves upon the regular curvy copter design. It has cuts that curve outwards more, allowing more moves to be made without having to force it to move. On top of that, this puzzle is an excellent puzzle to figure out how to solve on your own. You can figure it out one step at a time, each time going further and further into the scramble. This makes it a rather intuitive puzzle to solve. Along with everything else, this puzzle is very fun to solve. It doesn't get very repetitive, unlike other puzzles, and it turns great. This puzzle has a great price for what it is: a hybrid puzzle that is an absolute joy to solve.

review_title: Amazing cube for torturing a Rubik’s cube fan
review_text:
So I’ve got a buddy who loves solving traditional cubes and some of the harder variants. I originally bought him the gigaminx hoping he would struggle with it but he solved without issue so I knew I had to step it up.  I did some research into the hardest cubes and skewby copter kept being mentioned, after looking up the YouTube videos of it I knew it was the one.  Upon giving it to my friend some of his comments have been “it’s just a swirling vortex of colors”, “I will never solve this”, “Whoever invented this thing is a psycho”.   

 This cube has given haw truly given me a great level of entertainment as my friend still struggles to crack its code. I would 100% buy it again and I couldn't be happier.

This cube combines everything you want in a puzzle: being relaxing and fun (at least, after you've worked it out), being of high quality, turning well, being pretty, and just looking impressive. The stickers stay on perfectly without peeling of any kind, and their shades are excellent and really pop out.  

 It looks like an absolute MONSTER, but treat it like a marathon: long, but not a nightmare all the way through. The solve is pretty much entirely intuitive, which means every solve is unique but requires the same sets of strategies to move pieces around. The hardest part is working out the best order with which to solve the pieces. Just keep your cool, take your time, and you'll have hours of fun. 

 Git it. Right now.

An excellent upgrade to the Curvy Copter Plus: no overhang bandaging! Protruding jumbled pieces, even rotated face centers, don't collide with other pieces or catch easily. Even if you never use a skewb move, it is already superior to the Curvy Copter Plus in this way. 

 Note: I have the black plastic version with stickers. 

 Edge turning is amazingly smooth for a puzzle of this complexity. Skewb moves are rather stiff, even after lubrication, and require fairly precise alignment of pieces. Out of the box, it seemed somewhat over-lubricated, but very little seems to have remained on the sliding parts of the pieces. I put some weight 5 silicone oil on the pieces, which seems to help. 

 Drawbacks: some pieces that should have been glued are not. After reading and watching some other reviews, I consider this to be a design flaw. I didn't receive an answer to my question about this, even after a follow up email. 

 The wing edges come apart quite easily during a normal edge turn on an adjoining edge. One triangle of each wing edge is on a thin piece that slides into the other part that hooks into the core. After gluing the loose wing edges, the puzzle behaves very well. 

 Corner pieces are made of 3 parts that are not glued. This won't be a problem in normal use, but they can distort when pieces catch, possibly contributing to a pop. I guess you could lose reference to the color scheme if all of your corners come apart during disassembly. 

 Other reviews mention face center triangles popping easily, but I did not experience this. 

 There seems to be a fair amount of burrs and flash on the pieces that cause minor catches, but they seem to be smoothing out during break in.

There is internal bandaging which bandages the cube exactly the way the Bagua cube becomes bandaged by the orientation of the strip pieces. Awesome puzzle, but it does have it's flaws. Out of the box, I was surprised, it seemed to turn quite well but my oh my was I being fooled lol. I scrambled it up and after getting it back to cube shape I started noticing some issues. My two biggest problems were luckily fairly easy to fix. The center caps may as well have had fans behind them. Even the tiniest catch and one of them was popping off. Luckily the entire center piece is the correct color, so finding the proper place for the cap was easy. A few small pieces of paper under each cap fixed that pretty easily. However, the bigger issue was with the center pieces themselves. The friction inside between them and the core caused them to not rotate. So with a lot of turns, the pieces would rotate around the center rather than the center turning with them. This caused some odd lockups and just overall annoyance. Finally after getting more than tired of that issue, I busted out the tape and lube. I took each side of the puzzle off, taped together for easy reassembly. I cleaned and lubed the core and the pieces. After complete reassembly and a little bit of tension checking, I was astounded! It was like a completely different puzzle experience. 

 The puzzle solve is fun, although a little complicated. The indents on the stickerless kite shaped pieces make it easy to see where the bandaging might happen, that is once you figure out why the bandaging happens. 

 Overall, it's a very fun puzzle. Be prepared to spend a little bit of time and TLC making sure that it works a little better than out of the box. I'd say that if you're an avid solver that likes a new challenge then this is a great puzzle to grab. Not heavily algorithm based and the new ones you will need are fairly intuitive if you have a decent amount of puzzle knowledge.

This is another puzzle I really want to work. The idea is intriguing and seems really challenging to solve because of the jumbling. review_title: A great puzzle with a couple of problems
review_text: Sort of like a simplified Bagua cube but more stable. This looks like a more symmetrical (not-bandaged) version of the Unicorn Cube, which I liked (and what motivated me to buy it).

 Although it looks like Unicorn Cube, the corners do NOT twist.  You can play it like regular 3x3 cube (from my limited experience) but the unique thing is that instead of twisting faces by 90 degrees, you can turn by only 45 degrees.  This results in shape-modification and "bandaging" issues. 

 Sadly that is all almost everything I can say for sure... 

 This puzzle IS well lubricated out-of-the-box, but it still seems to catch when performing standard face turns... 

 Out-of-the-box the tension was very stiff (although well-lubricated).  I decided to  "exercise" the cube to HOPEFULLY make it easier to play... 

 I spent about 2 minutes turning a single face backwards and forwards (between 90 and 180 degrees)... no corner cutting or slice moves... just turning one face... and, without warning, the puzzle DISINTEGRATED! 

 I have NEVER experienced this before.  It is not like 1 piece popped out... multiple pieces popped at once and I was left with a lap-full of about 10 pieces... and I had no idea how to fix it... 

 I tried putting the pieces back, based on size/color, but the remainder of the puzzle continued to disintegrate.  So now I have 3/4 of a cube and about 20 tiny blocks in a pile of rubble! 

 I really WISH this would work, because it looks cool and fun... but mine self-destructed in less than 5 minutes.  Not recommended for anyone.

review_title: A must-have for fans of the mixup cube

This cube has been a ton of fun to work out and solve.  If you're comfortable with commutators and conjugates it's not too difficult to work out a few good algorithms.  It has a similar level of complexity to a 5x5, but with a very different feel.  It's basically a combination of a normal face turning 3x3 and a corner turner like a Redi cube or petal cube.  But the orbits of both puzzles overlap making for some interesting steps to the solve.  I also love the look of the stickerless version, the color scheme is unique and really works for this puzzle.  And given the unique shapes of the pieces, there are a lot of fun patterns you can make on it. 

 It's not a perfect cube by any means though.  The cube has a tendency to compress and squish in if you hold it with too much pressure; no doubt due to the numerous small pieces.  It takes a while to get used to get the hang of holding and turning it in a way that doesn't catch horribly.  Even after a month or so, it still feels like it catches a lot.  It also popped on me a few times.  But once you get used to handling it gingerly, the turning improves a lot.  It's definitely a small thing to overlook given the unique and fun design of this cube.

review_title: Amazing cube, but get the stickerless version.
review_text:
Difficulty: 7/10
 Playability: 8/10
 Quality: 9/10 

 OVERVIEW:
 The Unicorn Cube combines a crazy 3x3 with four corners that use Dino Cube moves. Because only half the corners use Dino turns, some turns are bandaged unless the pieces are moved to an orientation that allows them to turn. A good deal of planning ahead and setting up moves is necessary to solve the puzzle. The only algorithms needed to solve it are standard 3x3 ones, but you'll also need to find your own way of cycling pieces around the cube. A knowledge of bandaging is helpful. The only drawback is that, due to its complexity and the large number of small pieces, you won't be able to speed-solve this cube. Prepare to spend a good 20 minutes finishing it. Overall, it's well made, and a good challenge, but can catch due to its complexity. 

 PROS: Good challenge, sturdy build, and pleasing geometry. The 3x3 turns are very smooth.
 CONS: The Dino moves are somewhat catchy, and require alignment. Please keep in mind however that with a puzzle of this complexity, that's somewhat unavoidable. Additionally, for the stickered version, the small stickers are at risk of falling off due to the way the puzzle needs to be held; I recommend getting the stickerless version if possible.

I love the functionality of the puzzle!
 This is a fun addition to the standard Unicorn Cube. Sometimes there are catches when moving two faces in rapid succession. This is to be expected with so many moving pieces. My only real gripe is that some of the small stickers have begun to chip and peel. Higher quality stickers would be a big plus. I much prefer the look of stickered puzzles so I guess this is my own doing but I feel that I should be able to expect stickers that maintain quality for more than two solves before peeling and chipping.
 Overall, I am very happy with the purchase!

review_title: Looks Fun, but Needs Some Work.
review_text:
I've yet to scramble the cube, but it does look like it'll be a fun solve. As for the puzzle itself, I was a bit surprised by how cheap and low quality it looks and feels, given the price. This is my first MF8 brand puzzle and I wasn't expecting a speed cube, but I was expecting at least LanLan or Dayan level quality overall. I bought the stickerless version so I don't know if perhaps the stickered versions are made slightly better or if they perform the same, but I agree with Nic N. about how the plastic feels slightly above what you'd get from dollar store toys. It's thin and cheaply molded with various cosmetic defects in the plastic from several discoloration spots, some specks of black contamination, bad flow lines and some warpage (particularly on the center caps), heavy sink spots (especially on the small inner triangle pieces), but the worst part was that every piece had flash on it that was making the turning even worse. The small inner triangle pieces were the worst since I couldn't do dino cuts without them causing the center caps to go flying off. Out of the 50 puzzles I own, this is the only one that has ever popped on me (even if it's just the caps) and the only one I've had to modify. I disassembled the puzzle and spent 4 hours carefully trimming the flash off of each piece where it needed to be removed, then reassembled and tensioned the puzzle to a good point where it was loose enough to turn better, but not to the point where the small inner corner pieces would cause bad lockups. I don't think you need to trim every piece like I did, but I would at least recommend trimming the flash from the inner small corner pieces if you're having trouble doing dino turns or your caps are popping off too. Also, get some tape for the bottom layer to make reassembly much easier if you take it apart.
 The puzzle definitely needs lube, some breaking in, and should loosen up that flash on its own after a while with a few headaches and pops along the way. Now that I've modified the puzzle, it's turning much better than before. Not great, but better. I can almost get a layer to fully quarter turn with a firm finger flick. The dino turns are smoother now and not causing any more caps to pop off no matter how hard I try to force it to. I would give it a 3.5 as it is now and maybe a 4 after it full breaks in. I would still recommend this puzzle if you're interested in the solve and are willing to put in the time to break it in or do some slight modifications.

review_title: Unicorn Cube is fun and different but could be better
review_text:
The turning is a bit stiff, but not a problem unless you want to speed-solve.  Lock-ups are rare, unless you're going for speed.  My only serious complaint is the sticker quality: all the square stickers have visible creases and a few random ones were curling at the edges or had bubbles underneath.  Very minor complaint is the cut depth from the corners is a bit too shallow, leaving very tiny triangles around the centers (this is an artistic opinion, it doesn't affect how the puzzle plays). 

 This is a fun puzzle to solve!  It's something like a cross between a 3x3 and a 4x4.  If you can solve both of them, you can solve this by learning/thinking just a bit more. 

 For example, it has true center pieces, like a 3x3, but the edge pieces come in pairs like a 4x4.  You never get parity errors with edge pieces (common with 4x4 cube), but you can get a parity error which is impossible on any NxN cube: it is possible to solve the entire puzzle except one corner is turned wrong!  Finally, it is a "bandaged" cube because, in some states, some (or all) of the corners can not be twisted (from a solved state,  you can twist any corner). 

 Arguably a better puzzle than a 5x5 cube which just uses the same techniques of 3x3 and 4x4.  A good one to add to a collection.

review_title: It's not bad but it's got issues
review_text:
My take on this is... if you're a collector and you're dead set on getting a face-turning icosahedron for your collection, go ahead and pick this one up.  It's not great but it's good enough.  If, instead, all you're looking for is an impressive-looking puzzle with about this same level of difficulty, pick up one of the Bauhinia puzzles instead.  You'll have more fun with those. 

 The biggest issues here are with construction.  It straight-up does not want to turn counter-clockwise on any face — thankfully it is at least consistent in this regard but something about translating every R L' R' L into an R L2 R2 L was enough of a change to make me lose my place a lot and then I'd screw up and get set back a couple steps to fix the puzzle... and it just felt like the frustrating kind of challenge more than the satisfying kind because of this.  Its size is just large enough that it just kind of feels uncomfortable in your hands and you've really gotta get your whole wrist into the turn to get this thing to move.  And even when I was turning it clockwise-only I had multiple pops to fix over the course of a solve. 

 But those drawbacks aside, the challenge of figuring out how to get the pieces in place is a fun and approachable one.  Being comfortable with commutators is necessary but you'll be able to unlock its secrets.  Experience with redi-minx, face-turning octahedron, and (obviously) Bauhinia helped me out with my solve but I wouldn't say those are strict prerequisites.

review_title: Please Become Recognized and Mass Produced
review_text:
As of 2025, FTOs are gaining popularity and when it becomes an official WCA event there will be four face turning 3x3 plantonic solids: 3x3, Megaminx, Pyraminx (Ig both), and FTO. It would neat to see this become an official event. 

 As of the cube itself, I tried it before, it was really stiff, could somehow jumble, and it is equivalent to a megaminx to the 3x3 but to a FTO.

I bought this with my prize money from winning thecubicle.us' essay contest. I have to say, I was a bit hesitant about spending it all on one puzzle, but after having it for about a month, I have concluded that this is without a doubt worth every penny. 

 The turning is phenomenal out of the box/case, its incredibly stable and easy to turn. I spent about an hour stickering it, 10 minutes scrambling it, and am currently about halfway through the solve. If you're going to get this puzzle, I'd recommend trying to solve it yourself, without a tutorial. This thing is considered the hardest-to-solve mass produced twisty puzzle for a reason, and figuring out algorithms is the best part! 

 If you want a fun, difficult puzzle of high quality, this it it.

THE BASICS
  Out of the box movement is excellent enough that I have not felt the need to apply any lube. I have yet to encounter any catching or popping. It doesn't seem to jumble or want to jumble however I really haven't tried to find jumbling moves. The stickers seem high quality enough to withstand regular use pending the user is not forceful or strong handed with the puzzle. 

 THE ALGORITHMS
  There are many ways to approach this cube and many ways to move the different pieces around. It is here I have to agree with Mr. SuperAntonioVivaldi in recommending that you, the owner of this puzzle, take the time on your own to find/create the move sets you feel are needed to move pieces around. I spend nearly a week just with studying and moving the puzzle around to try and find new ways and I was constantly amazed at how I was able to find new ways to achieve different results. 

 THE VERDICT
  If you are up for a challenge here is one right in this 20 sided wonder. I can say that it was worth every penny and more.

review_title: Very smooth turning, but occasional internal misalignment.
review_text: Got my puzzle yesterday. Turns very well, movement is very smooth, and fully functional as advertised. Has a springy feel due to the internal mechanism, which allows a fair bit of stretching without popping or breaking (just don't overdo it!).  However, the internal mechanism occasionally gets misaligned, and allowed turns get jammed. Backing off and jittering it fixes the alignment and allows the turn afterwards. Other than this occasional issue, very satisfied with this puzzle.  Very interesting solve due to the uniqueness conferred by the 2x3x4 dimensions.

The 2x3x4 is a shapeshifting brick cuboid puzzle. 

 The turning is worse than I expected: the two outer layers (1x2x3 faces) are much looser than the one middle layer (turning a 2x2x3 block). Months ago, I wrote that while tensioning the puzzle, I thought that it was going to explode from an internal lock-up, but recently, it actually did pop. I took apart the puzzle completely, and realized that it was very hard to put back together, but I was able to tension and turn the puzzle better afterwards. 

 If you ever need to put together the puzzle, SuperAntonioVivaldi's tutorial is a great help. Also get a flashlight if you can't see the internal pieces clearly, otherwise you might assemble the puzzle but not be able to turn it afterwards. 

 The solve itself is very interesting, if you never solved a fully-functional brick cuboid puzzle before. But, since it's a small puzzle, there's not as much challenge to it as a larger cuboid, and so the solve ends fairly quickly. 

 The fairly minimal paper box the puzzle comes in is quite pretty, and makes me relate the puzzle to a deck of cards when it comes to its portability. 

 In summary, I would only recommend this puzzle to collectors, and anyone enthusiastic about smaller cuboid puzzles who does not mind mediocre turning quality and the potential risk of having to do a tough re-assembly.

If you try to turn this thing like a speedcube you're setting yourself up for failure. It's remarkably stable, and when it catches you can usually carefully persuade it to do what you need it to, assuming you have the updated version that doesn't internally bandage. Catches have become less and less frequent as I've done more solves, leading me to believe the culprit may have just been a bit of plastic flash that needed to be worn down. Overall, it's a fantastic solve that manages to be more difficult than most other puzzles its size. I highly recommend it as your first really challenging cuboid, after you've mastered the 3x3x4.

Again by far the most difficult puzzle to assemble i've ever encountered.

I would still be careful when turning it to prevent the tiny stickers from peeling off, and to prevent pops (not that I've had it pop on me, but in the off chance it does pop, it WILL explode completely due to the nature of its mechanism). review_title: Gorgeous Puzzle, Amazingly Engineered with a Couple of Issues
review_text:
This is one of the most beautiful puzzles ever designed. The engineering and craftsmanship are incredible and complex. However that complexity lends itself to some unavoidable issues when it comes to turnability. The core is a sturdy spherical megaminx, the entire rest of the puzzle is made up of many interconnected pieces that move along a track system. If anything is slightly out of alignment the puzzle will lock and occasionally derail. The puzzle comes lubricated from the factory and after few days of twisting, the turning does get a bit smoother when properly aligned. 

 The other main issue is that the corner pieces are only held in by the pressure of the surrounding puzzle. Corner pieces have a tendency to fall out during a solve. Since they're multi-sided they can't just be put back in, unless you happen to see the exact orientation before one pops out. By the time I solved the puzzle I was down to about 9 corners left in place. 

 I love the idea of this puzzle and I love the appearance of this puzzle. When it comes to usability it's more frustrating that fun. It really is well made though. Hopefully someone thinks it's worthwhile to figure out a way to improve the turnability issue and releases an updated version.

This puzzle is BRUTAL.  Definitely pushed my own solving abilities to their limits.  It's tough enough to figure out how to manipulate the pieces, and once you've wrapped your head around that part there is just so much puzzle to be solved, so throw on some podcasts or audio books because you're going to be at this thing for a while. 

 Turn quality is serviceable, but it could be better.  It catches a lot — I didn't have any problems with popping but when you're trying to remember how to undo your extensive setup moves, having to stop to fight the puzzle adds the wrong kind of difficulty. 

 I'm glad I got this puzzle, it was satisfying to finally get this thing solved, but TBH I don't see myself getting a whole lot of replay out of it because it's just a bit much. 

 If you're reading wondering if you could take this puzzle on... this is considerably more challenging than a Megaminx or Gigaminx.  I'd say a similar challenge level to a Rua, but with many more pieces to deal with.

I took a star off because the corner pieces often pop, as do the small triangle pieces occasionally. Fortunately they're easy enough to pop back in, but that can slow you down if you're in the middle of a very long sequence. And you may be executing some very long sequences because this puzzle is extremely difficult -- easily the most difficult puzzle I own and probably too difficult for the casual cuber. But I'm glad I resisted the temptation to give up and look online for a solution... it was incredibly satisfying crossing the finish line to the solved state. If you're looking for a challenge, you will definitely not be disappointed by this puzzle.

Like most mf8 products, this is not a speed cube.  That said, it is one of the best moving mf8 products I have come across!  Movement was pretty good out of the box, and improved with a little lube.  The only concern while turning if catching one of the corner pieces.  If you do so too quickly, the corner cap pops off its stick and you have to click it back on.  Most misalignment issues can be prevented by solving on a flat surface or using full-palm grips on both sides of the puzzle.  Once you get used to the quirks of the hardware, the solve is interesting.  First set the corners, then three-cycle all the edges into place, triple-three-cycle the centres into place, then spend a long time three-cycling the inner triangles into place.  I think if the corners were tweaked (solid, with forgiving corners, etc), this could be even better.  This was a puzzle I was glad to have obtained! 🙋🏼‍♀️ 

 Side note: mine came already stickered with a spare set in the box.  The stickering job was hanging over the edges on many pieces, and the five faces around the grey side needed to be reapplied one face clockwise to match the standard colour scheme.  I think I had to reposition about half the stickers overall to get them acceptable.  They simply were applied in the wrong place, and had not shifted during transit (like we would sometimes see many years ago due to heat, lube, and bad adhesive).  Finding it stickered increased the “wow” out of the box, but having to peel and place took a bit to find the exact angle that wouldn’t cause the tips to bend, crease, or not stick anymore.  (At least I had a backup set of stickers in the box)

This is actually a corner turning dodecahedron, unlike what the description says. This makes it mechanically equivalent to a face turning icosahedron. It is very beautiful, is quite satisfying to solve, and, like other corner turning puzzles, its solve primarily involves commutators and setup moves. It'll be fun to work out if you've mastered puzzles like the elite skewb. 

 This puzzle, as you can see in the picture, is also capable of jumbling, though this does not add any additional challenge to the solve unlike on the Curvy Copter. Its turning is satisfyingly crunchy but very catchy, which can cause the tiny triangle pieces to pop. I've lost one of these pieces because of this, and this is a big problem because now other pieces are starting to pop out too. Sticker quality is relatively poor, and they often peel at the corners. The small triangle stickers are most annoying but haven't fallen off so far - I've owned this puzzle for 6 months at the time for writing. But aside from that, the puzzle appears to be very well built.  And it turns nicely when you get it moving.  It comes unstickered which is annoying.  But if you put a little time and effort into it, it's not that bad. 

 The puzzle is difficult.  This is not something for a beginner.  It will take some time to wrap your head around what order to solve the pieces.  I personally haven't solved this yet, but I am enjoying the journey. 

 Oh and the puzzle also jumbles similar to the helicopter cube.  And while the helicopter allows you to jumble swap two pieces into different orbits, this pentagram allows you to jumble swap three sets of pieces.  At this point, I'm not sure if it is completely necessary to jumble swap them back in order to solve this, but that would jack up the difficulty so much more if you do.

This parity comes in 2 forms; one green square on the all blue face and one blue on the all green, assuming everything else on the puzzle is solved. If these 2 squares are directly opposite each other on the puzzle, you have 'snake eyes' ; that is head heavy, tail light. If the 2 squares are at opposite ends of the two 5x4 faces the puzzle is balanced.                  As far as I can tell, you can't solve this parity without switching from the balanced form to the snake eyes formation. This is easy and you should be able to switch back and fourth between these two forms if you were able to get this far. Switch to snake eye form. With everything else solved on the puzzle, apply the algorithm to the top two layers. This algorithm is the one used on your 3x3x4 and similar puzzles when none of the colors on the edges or corners match. Practice on your 3x3x4 until you're confident. Now apply it to the top two layers of your 3x4x5 remembering the outer corners and edges are 2 pieces fused together to make one piece; so don't let the shape shifting throw you; it's the exact same algorithm. Now bring the mono-colored pieces on the two 5x4 faces back to snake eyes. Now switch from snake eyes to the balanced form and apply the same algorithm to the same top 2 layers. The puzzle is now easily solved using moves and algorithms you already know. Keep in mind this parity is tough and makes this cuboid harder than the 4x4x6 cuboid even though they are much different.

review_title: Not actually fully functional and sometimes bandages layers together
review_text:
I had no complaints until I started encountering certain configurations where the 2 outer extended layers of the 5 side bandage together even when in the proper shape.  It sounds like this was a big problem with the mf8 2x3x4 as well several years ago, and required replacing some internal parts to fix it, though the 2x3x4 parts were eventually installed correctly from the factory and supposedly isn't an issue anymore.  It appears this same factory fix has NOT yet been addressed for the 3x4x5, so it is not actually fully functional out of the box. 

 The bandaging is pretty infrequent and doesn't happen nearly as often as the original bad version of the 2x3x4 appeared to, but when you do encounter it it will inevitably be in the middle step of the brick parity algorithm when it hurts the most and prevents you from finishing the alg.  You can try cycling through some corner cycles algs that shapeshift and resolve the corners to see if that unbandages it, but it's inconsistent and doesn't always work. 

 So every brick parity alg requires crossing your fingers when you get to the middle slice move and hope it isn't bandaged.  Luckily it only happens once every several parity algs, but happens enough to be extremely irritating.  So far I've only seen the bandaging between the outer 2 layers on the 5 side - I haven't seen it between layers on the 4 side or know if the internals would actually allow it there in certain configuration or not. 

 There is information online about the bandaging on the original bad release of the 2x3x4, but seems to be very little information online about the 3x4x5 bandaging or how to work around it, and as of 2020 the 3x4x5 seems to still be a very niche puzzle.

My cube broke while I was cubing and it is generally a good cube. But when it popped it one of the center pieces came off and cracked

THE PROBLEM: The springs are very sharp and bite away at the center pieces. A few sides of the cube suddenly started making loud grinding noises, and that's because the spring's sharp end is scraping the plastic off the internals (see image below). 

 THE SOLUTION: rub the sharp ends of each spring on sandpaper (I used 220 grit) until the ends are rounded off and don't feel sharp anymore. It worked great for me. 

 Performance: cube is too tight out of the box and hard to turn. When loosened, the cube speeds up drastically and starts to corner cut well. It's stable, lightweight and has a reasonable magnet strength. I like it a lot. 

 Size: at 60mm, this 5x5 is about the same size as many 4x4 cubes, which is crazy. The compact size feels comfortable, but the outer layers are slim and sometimes hard to grip. 

 Overall, great value for $12. However, you must be willing to modify the springs to stop the cube from destroying itself internally. If not, look elsewhere (QiYi MS 5x5 may be a good option, but I've never tried it)

review_title: good 5x5, but 1 small problem with easy fix
review_text:
out of the box, the cube reminded me a lot of the meilong 4 m because it was fast and swooshy, the tensions were perfect and corner-cutting was great. 

 whilst I was setting up the cube I noticed that the center lip of the cube was getting grinded by the bottom of the spring and little plastic chunks were coming off, this is most likely due to the springs being low quality with a rough end on the springs. some of the ways to fix this would be to either add a washer to the bottom, add some thick lube like weight 5, or what I recommend, lubicle black, sand down the end of the spring to smoothed it out, or all of the above. 

 i set up the pieces with a lot of lubicle 1 and quit a bit of silk and weight 5 in the inner layers to make 3x3 stage more enjoyable as the inner layers are being held together by both the magnets and thicker lube. 

 in conclusion, I think that this is a great 5x5 for its price but there is just 1 small problem with the core but there is an easy fix. overall this cube is great and I dropped my times by about 25 seconds. 

 I highly recommend this cube as long as if you are willing to fix the core

I average ~2:40 on 7x7, and after adding few mods, setup, and lots of break in, this cube can become the best on the market by a solid margin, significantly outperforming the AoFu WRM. Out of the box, the cube is tight, fast, and can be prone to catches due to poorer corner cutting than premium 7x7s. 

 I added a ball-core to this cube, along with a Florian mod to improve corner cutting, and a weight reduction mod of the pieces. I loosened the cube quite a bit, lubed it with a light Angstrom setup (Gravitas, Dignitas) on the core/pieces and DNM-37, and broke it in over the course of a few hundred solves.  

 Now, the cube is light, stable, lightning fast, corner cutting is pretty good, and the magnets are the perfect strength. This cube is now so satisfying and light/effortless to turn that the AoFu is sluggish, heavy, and almost…tiring to solve on. I could never imagine switching back to it. 

 It is true that the cube requires lots of set up/modding to become amazing. Out of box, it’s still good for a budget cube, but definitely doesn’t perform as well as the AoFu, so if you’re someone who isn’t experienced in/doesn’t want to do extensive set up and modding, I’d go for the AoFu. With the mods/set up mentioned above though, in my opinion this cube far outperforms the AoFu, and easily becomes the best 7x7 on the market by a wide margin. If you’re willing to do the work to get it to that point, this will quickly become an extremely rewarding cube that only keeps getting better with more solves.

The Short Version: This is arguably the best 7x7 available stock at any price point, and unquestionably the best 7x7 if you mod it. 

 The Long Version: 

 I'm not a world-class 7x7 solver.  I average right around 3 minutes, so I'm not bad but also not great.  However, I know enough fast people who share my opinion that I feel valid enough to post this :).  The only competition this cube has is the Aofu WRM, so here's how they stack up.  The Meilong V2 is much lighter than the Aofu, which is a big advantage during long sessions.  It's SIGNIFICANTLY faster, which matters a ton on big cubes.  The magnets are weaker in this cube than the Aofu, which isn't all bad, but on top of that the corner cutting is noticeably worse on this than the Aofu.  I had to loosen the cube significantly and adjust my turning style a lot to make it work - It took 20-30 solves to get used to the way it performs.  The other odd thing about this cube is that the magnets in the 2nd layer are much stronger than outers and 3rd layers.  Why?  Who knows.  It got better after some setup on my puzzle, but it is noticeable.  When you hold and solve this cube, you can just tell it's "cheaper" than the Aofu.  It feels a bit hollow, less solid, and the plastic isn't as nice. 

 On big cubes, light and fast matter A LOT.  The Aofu has better magnets, corner-cutting, and "quality" than this puzzle, but the speed and weight of this puzzle make the Aofu feel like a sluggish brick by comparison.  After getting used to the turning style, this cube made 7x7 a lot of fun, and I dropped a solid 10-15 seconds off my global within 100 solves.  I can't go back to the Aofu now, it feels like way too much work to turn compared to this cube. 

 The biggest problem with this cube is corner cutting.  There are 2 solutions to that: loosen the cube (which makes it less stable), or do a mod so that it corner cuts better.  Several world-class solvers have done both.  If you do a Florian mod to this puzzle (sanding down the tips on corners and outer wings), the corner cutting gets significantly better.  If you florian mod, loosen tensions, AND install a ball core?  This puzzle goes from better than the Aofu to WAY WAY WAY better. 

 If you are looking for a 7x7 and don't own one yet, get this one.  It's the best price vs. quality on the market.  If you're looking for the best 7x7, why not get this one - it's only $20!  If you're a hobbyist and have time to modify your puzzles, definitely do it for this one. 

 Now if only MoYu would put the corner cutting and quality of the Aofu and the speed/weight of the Meilong together - seems like they should be able to since it's the same company LOL

review_title: The orange and the peach are annoying.
review_text:
So the first fruit cube set also comes with a lemon, I bought both sets and now I have two lemons I guess, oops. I think this set would've been better if it didn't have the lemon and a few dollars cheaper. 

 The main problem though is the orange and the peach! Compared to all the other fruit cubes which are cute and easy to solve in a minute or less, these two are very tedious and difficult. They're like 3x3 ghost cubes, except some pieces are duplicates (the orange has more duplicate pieces than the peach) and they have some symmetry revolving around 2 opposite corners. Also it's just impossible to do any look-ahead, solving the cross takes a few minutes on it's own. I believe I keep running into a parity case where one of my centers is rotated 90 degrees, and I can't figure out what piece swap or cycle is necessary to fix it. The instructions do tell you one parity case where you need to swap two duplicate edges, but that doesn't really describe which pieces should be swapped and their algorithm still scrambles the top layer and isn't very helpful. And anyways I seem to be getting a different parity case which isn't in the instructions. So I end up spending 20 minutes scrambling it and solving it again, hoping not to encounter parity on the last layer, and it's just very un-fun to solve. A regular ghost cube is a lot more enjoyable for me. 

 Looks great in a fake fruit bowl on the kitchen counter tho! So if you want it for the novelty, it still gets a recommendation from me. Just don't scramble the orange or the peach!
